articles.title: Ukraine intercepting more Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drones, General Staff says
articles.body:
Ukraine's air defenses have intercepted nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with interception rates reaching 80% during some attacks, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces said.
Fighter jets, including F-16s, Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29s, play a significant role in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, according to the General Staff.
It did not mention interceptions rates of the more advanced Geran-5 drone.
Ukraine is also working to strengthen its short-range air defenses amid a shortage of surface-to-air missiles.
These defenses include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft systems, newer platforms such as Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups operating across Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped with machine guns and man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), which Ukrainian troops have successfully used to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.
The General Staff said Ukraine is also seeking cheaper ways to counter the threat, including testing new interceptor drones. Some of the systems being tested have already shot down dozens of Russian jet-powered Geran drones, according to the military.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones to attack Kyiv and the surrounding region since late summer, adding to the threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles.
The newer Geran-5 drones fly higher and faster than other drones, making them significantly harder to intercept. Their growing numbers have also challenged Ukraine's existing interceptor drones, which have proved effective against slower Russian drones.
Ukraine is racing to develop faster interceptors to counter the evolving threat, while Russia is expanding production of jet-powered drones.
Ukraine previously achieved interception rates of around 95% against conventional Shahed-type drones.

articles.title: How the War in Iran Could Escalate
articles.body:
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Before the mother of all bombs
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao, were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “finishing the job” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
Denying Trump a short war
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain, the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned. The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “smuggling” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali, an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi, strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
Widening the map
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. In Iraq, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran-backed militia, has threatened to fight if Iran faced an existential threat. The conflict could also extend to Europe through indirect operations.
There may already have been attempts in this vein: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a suspected September plot near RAF Fairford, a base used by U.S. bombers, was “almost certainly” directed by the IRGC. Tehran denies involvement, but the incident raises the prospect of covert operations against American military assets beyond the Middle East.
Tehran is also preparing for the possibility of a ground operation inside Iran. According to Iranian Army Ground Forces commander Ali Jahanshahi, more than 50 units are deployed along the borders, from the northwest to the Makran coast, and abandoned airfields have been identified as potential enemy landing sites. Iranian security forces have also conducted preemptive operations against Baluch armed groups in the southeast and launched drone and artillery strikes in Kurdish border areas amid concerns that they could open an internal front during an external attack.
A war meant to be the last
Both the U.S. and Iran run the risk of serious misjudgment. The U.S. may believe it can be master of the scope and duration of a war, only to find that Iran holds the key. This power means Iran need not let the conflict end quickly or painlessly.
For its part, Tehran—which survived the fierce exchanges that began in late February, continued through April, and have since become more regionalized—may be convinced that a wider conflict this time again would establish lasting deterrence. But conditions that made this strategy relatively effective in the past have changed, partly because of Iran’s own actions. The more Tehran expands its targets, the more it risks turning neighbors that sought to stay out of the conflict into supporters of its defeat. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have reportedly agreed to coordinate their military support on behalf of anti-Houthi forces in Yemen, while Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has offered to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. For the Gulf monarchies, the stakes are becoming existential: either Iran’s leverage is broken, or their access to world markets will remain dependent on Iranian restraint.
In this way, a war intended to deter future American attacks could instead strengthen a regional consensus that Iran must be dealt a serious blow rather than accommodated or bargained with.
Ultimately, diplomacy remains the only way to prevent the gap between American and Iranian perceptions and risk calculus from triggering another, potentially even more costly round of confrontation. Without it, Washington could launch a limited strike expecting a quick exit, or Tehran could strike first fearing an imminent attack. Either scenario could trigger a prolonged regional war that the U.S. wishes to avoid and a growing alliance against the Islamic Republic for which Iran would pay a price.

articles.title: One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
articles.body:
One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
A Ukrainian drone strike on a passenger bus bound for Moscow has killed one person and wounded several others, according to Evgeny Balitsky, the governor of Russia’s Zaporozhye Region, where the attack took place.
The attack was reported on Tuesday morning near the town of Primorsk, on the Sea of Azov between the towns of Melitopol and Berdyansk. The area, which Ukraine claims as its territory, lies within the zone of so-called “middle strikes,” where Ukrainian forces have regularly launched drone attacks on purported Russian military and logistics targets using the Starlink satellite system for guidence.
Balitsky said 31 people were aboard the bus, which was traveling from Simferopol, the capital of the Crimean Republic, to Moscow. He said the wounded were taken to hospital, while other survivors were provided with food and accommodation.
The incident comes amid a dispute between Kiev and Elon Musk over Ukraine’s use of his Starlink satellite communications network for military purposes.
Musk has accused Ukraine of abusing Starlink for deadly “middle strike” operations, saying the system was intended as a civilian communications service rather than an offensive military tool. He contrasted it with Starshield, SpaceX’s military-oriented satellite service developed for US government customers.
Media reports and statements by officials have offered conflicting accounts of whether Kiev has direct access to Starshield or relies primarily on civilian Starlink terminals. Kiev has accused Musk and US President Donald Trump of imposing speed restrictions on Starlink terminals that effectively prevented their use on fast-moving platforms involved in middle strikes. Russian media reported a sharp decline in such attacks this month.
While the Ukrainian military depends heavily on Starlink communications, it has other means of conducting strikes deep inside Russia, where Starlink does not normally operate. Long-range drones and missiles can follow pre-programmed routes and use AI-driven final stage guidance to strike Russian energy infrastructure and other stationary targets.
The Starlink dispute has unfolded amid wider tensions between Washington and Kiev over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The Trump administration has repeatedly asked Kiev to curb strikes on refineries amid concerns about rising fuel prices, while Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has rejected claims that Ukraine’s campaign is contributing to the increase.
Global energy markets are under pressure from several factors, including the US war on Iran, the Ukraine conflict and depleted strategic reserves amid tight crude supplies.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia fires over 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, region in two weeks
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia fires over 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, region in two weeks
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a video address, Ukrinform reports.
“And just now, in October alone – since October 14 – there have already been several Russian ballistic missile attacks. Essentially, in two weeks, more than 100 ballistic missiles have been launched against Kyiv and the Kyiv region. We are doing everything possible to protect our energy sector, to protect our infrastructure and our logistics. The task is extremely difficult,” Zelensky said.
The head of state thanked Ukraine’s partners who provide support on time but noted that delays, including in the delivery of missiles for Patriot systems, are making it difficult for Ukraine to protect itself against Russian ballistic missiles.
“If our partners’ support for Ukraine remained just as strong – particularly when it comes to our Patriots and other air defense capabilities – Ukraine would be in a completely different position – a much better one diplomatically as well,” Zelensky said.
The President stressed that Russia continues to attack Ukrainian logistics and urban infrastructure. In particular, during a recent strike on Kyiv, a university campus, residential buildings, a metro station and metro lines were damaged. Russian forces also struck the Southern Bridge, one of the capital’s key logistical arteries.
According to Zelensky, Russian attacks are continuing not only against Kyiv, but also against Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy and Kherson.
“It is important that the world sees this, that our partners see it in the United States, on which almost everything concerning Patriots depends, so that we get answers and the necessary authorizations from the Pentagon for Patriot supplies,” the President said.
He added that Ukraine is working to secure new support packages from its partners to protect the energy system, infrastructure and logistics.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 27, commenting on another Russian attack involving ballistic missiles, President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that Russia’s targets are energy facilities, logistics and ordinary urban infrastructure.
The day before, he said that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missile supplies for Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: Scandal-hit German special forces prepare for war with Russia – commander
articles.body:
Scandal-hit German special forces prepare for war with Russia – commander
Germany’s elite special forces are preparing for a potential large-scale war with Russia, the unit’s commander has told Bild. The remarks come amid ongoing tensions between Moscow and NATO over the Ukraine conflict, with German officials warning that the country’s military must be ready for a possible confrontation by the end of the decade.
The highly secretive unit, known as Kommando Spezialkrafte (KSK), is comparable to Britain’s SAS or the US Green Berets. According to a report from its base in southwestern Germany published on Monday, the commandos are adjusting their training to counter Russian forces equipped with tanks, artillery, drones and electronic warfare capabilities, including in extreme cold.
“We are orienting ourselves very specifically toward the adversary Russia,” KSK Commander Brigadier General Andreas Kuhne said, adding that his soldiers would have to be prepared to “remain in the field much longer,” potentially “with no end in sight,” if war broke out.
Kuhne also said the unit was preparing to carry out missions before conventional German forces entered combat. “When the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania starts its engines in a real emergency, we want to have already completed our job,” he told Bild.
According to the newspaper, only about a third of the KSK’s roughly 1,500 personnel are commandos, while the rest serve in administrative and support roles.
The unit has been rocked by a series of far-right extremism scandals in recent years. In 2017, prosecutors launched an investigation following reports that soldiers had performed Nazi salutes, listened to far-right music and offered a woman as a “prize” at a farewell party for an outgoing company commander.
In 2018, investigations exposed an underground far-right network involving German military and security personnel, some of whom allegedly discussed plans to kill political opponents in the event of a breakdown of public order. 
In 2020, police discovered a large cache of weapons, ammunition, explosives and Nazi memorabilia at the property of a KSK sergeant major. Some of the ammunition was suspected of having been stolen from Bundeswehr stocks.
The scandals prompted then-Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer to disband one of the KSK’s four commando companies, the 2nd Company, and introduce sweeping reforms. The special forces command itself remained operational.
Speaking to Bild, Kuhne acknowledged that disciplinary and conduct-related incidents within the unit had become “extremely rare,” but had not disappeared entirely. He insisted that misconduct would no longer be tolerated or covered up.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional military force in response to what he describes as threats from Russia. His government has prioritized defense spending and military assistance to Ukraine despite acknowledging that the German economy is in a “structural crisis.”
In July, The Telegraph and Die Welt reported that Berlin was preparing a secret plan to override potential resistance from regional governments to the deployment of NATO troops toward Russia’s borders.
Merz’s military ambitions come amid declining public support for his government. According to an INSA poll published by Bild this week, the chancellor ranked last among 20 prominent German politicians. The surging opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) won state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, while the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) emerged as the largest party in Berlin’s election.
Russia has repeatedly denied having plans to attack NATO countries. In August, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed reports alleging that Moscow intended to attack alliance members as “scare stories” that had “nothing to do with reality” or Russia’s intentions.

articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 55 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 57 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least four and wounded at least 55 others over the past day, Ukrainian authorities said on Oct. 27, as Russia launched an overnight missile and drone blitz against the capital, Kyiv.
Russian attacks hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, disrupting metro services, as well as a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people were injured in the latest Russian attack on the capital, Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia attacked Kyiv with an unspecified number of S-400 and Iskander ballistic missiles, launched from Bryansk Oblast, and with 280 strike drones of various types, 69 of which were jet-powered.
Two ballistic missiles and 255 Russian strike drones, including 56 jet-powered drones, were shot down by Ukrainian air defense or suppressed by electronic warfare.
There were 25 locations reported struck by Russian munitions in the capital, as well as 16 locations that were struck by falling debris from downed missiles and drones.
In Chernihiv Oblast, six people, including a 12-year-old child, were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Chernivtsi Oblast, two men were lightly njured in a Russian drone strike, according to regional authorities.
In Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed and 22 people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to local authorities. These included a 62-year-old nurse who was injured when a Russian "Molniya" drone struck a hospital in the city of Kherson.
In Sumy Oblast, three people were injured in Russian drone strikes, according to regional authorities.
In Zaporizhia Oblast, five people were injured as a result of Russian attacks, including a 17-year-old boy, according to regional authorities.

articles.title: Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses have been intercepting nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with the interception rate reaching 80% during some attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine, adding a faster-moving threat to the Shahed-type drones Moscow deploys against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine is working to improve interception rates while reducing the cost of countering these aerial threats amid shortages of surface-to-air missiles.
The General Staff’s update did not mention interception rates for Russia’s more advanced Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
F-16s, Mirage jets help intercept Russian drones
According to the General Staff, tactical aviation plays a significant role in destroying Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine uses F-16s, French Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29 fighters to intercept them.
The military is also strengthening what it calls “short-range air defense” as Ukraine faces a shortage of guided anti-aircraft missiles. These systems include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft guns, newer Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin systems, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups deployed by different branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped not only with machine guns and supporting equipment but also with man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS). Ukrainian troops have been successfully using these missiles to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, the General Staff said.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones
Ukraine tests cheaper drone interceptors
Ukraine is also seeking to lower the cost of countering Russian aerial attacks by testing new interceptor drones.
According to the General Staff, some models have already downed dozens of Russian Geran jet-powered drones. The military did not provide further details about the interceptor models or the number of drones destroyed.
The rising interception rate reflects Ukraine’s efforts to adapt its air defenses to Russia’s evolving drone campaign while preserving scarce and expensive air-defense missiles for threats that require them.

articles.title: European countries with the largest defense budgets name Russia their main security threat and pledge continued support for Ukraine
articles.body:
European countries with the largest defense budgets name Russia their main security threat and pledge continued support for Ukraine
Defense ministers from the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Poland, and France met in Paris on October 26 as members of the E5 group — the countries with the largest defense budgets — to discuss support for Ukraine ahead of winter.
After the meeting, the ministers named Russia the main long-term threat to European security and pledged to keep supporting Ukraine despite Washington’s warming relations with Moscow.
“Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability,” the final statement reads. Russia’s war against Ukraine and intensifying hybrid attacks in Europe “do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion. On the contrary, they strengthen our determination to pursue the efforts already undertaken to safeguard the integrity and security of Allied territory,” the ministers said.
The ministers pledged to continue backing Ukraine but announced no new military or financial aid packages, Bloomberg said. During the meeting, they limited themselves to reaffirming earlier commitments.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stressed that the allies would work to preserve U.S. support for Ukraine: “We will do everything we can to ensure that the U.S. also supports Ukraine with supplies, as well as with intelligence and satellite data.”
The latest deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the United States is forcing Europe to consider how to help Ukraine without American support, Bloomberg said. Pistorius said the E5 countries are also working with Ukraine on their own air defense system meant to supplement the U.S. Patriot systems.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated sharply amid a fuel crisis. Donald Trump first demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian fuel infrastructure, and when a cease-fire could not be reached, he eased sanctions against Russia, allowing diesel fuel to be sold on the world market.
In response, Volodymyr Zelensky accused Trump of trying to force Ukraine into capitulation, saying the United States is delaying shipments of missiles for Patriot air defense systems and restricting the operation of Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Israel Heads to the Polls as Netanyahu Battles to Stay in Power
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, appear short of an outright victory, initial exit polls indicate.
The polls show Eisenkot’s opposition bloc with a narrow edge over Netanyahu and his allies, though they suggest that neither side will emerge with a clear path to a governing majority.
Still, opposition leaders cast the initial poll results as an evident rebuke of Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who is facing one of the most consequential tests of his political career.
Eisenkot wrote on social media shortly following the release of the preliminary exit polls that “the preliminary poll results point to complete distrust in Netanyahu” and contended that “if these are the final results, this is a victory.”
Opposition leader Yair Lapid and Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s Democrats party, treated the initial polls as an even stronger marker of the opposition’s success.
“Don't let them confuse you: The Netanyahu bloc suffered a harsh defeat,” Lapid posted. "This is a total collapse and the public told them to get lost and go home.”
“The public has spoken, it has fired the Netanyahu government,” Golan wrote.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister and head of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, meanwhile expressed hope that Netanyahu's bloc would ultimately prevail, pointing to differences between exit polls. “The night is still young,” Ben-Gvir said Tuesday evening.
Israelis flocked to polling stations earlier in the day to decide Netanyahu’s political fate.
From 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time on Tuesday (1 a.m. to 4 p.m. EDT), Israelis were able to cast votes for representatives in the Knesset. Numbers from Israel's Central Elections Committee reflected a strong turnout, with 77.7% of eligible voters reported to have cast their ballots by 10 p.m., local time—the highest turnout logged since 1999.
Netanyahu was joined by his wife Sara as he cast his own ballot just after midday, at a polling station in a Jerusalem school. “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed,” Netanyahu told reporters after voting. “We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.”
Not long after, Netanyahu told his supporters that "buses are heading to the polling stations and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements." Complaining that "the right-wing strongholds are not waking up," he again urged people to go out and vote.
Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had submitted a request to the Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past 10 p.m. The committee later announced it would not be extending voting hours past the scheduled closing time.
This is the first election in the country since the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Palestinian militant group Hamas and the subsequent Israeli war in the Gaza Strip. Since then, Israel under Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military campaign across the Middle East—going to war with Iran, backing settler attacks and displacement in the West Bank, and carrying out strikes against militant groups in Lebanon and Yemen.
The election was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and Israelis’ willingness to change course amid uncertainty.
Read More: Israel's Choice
“I hope this will be a true holiday for democracy,” Isaac Herzog, the Israeli head of state, told reporters from a polling station in Rehavia, where he and his wife voted. “No one can be allowed to spoil or undermine it.”
Here’s what to know:
Who is in the running?
Two main political blocs are contending to form Israel’s next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party. The coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, such as Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionism-Zehut led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich. Their ultranationalist policies have found an audience in younger right-wing Israelis.
On the other side are the Jewish-led opposition movements—with Eisenkot and the centrist Yashar (Straight) party at the forefront. Eisenkot, who entered politics in 2022, joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet after the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. But after having lost a son in combat in Israel’s wars, Eisenkot left his post in 2024. Two of his nephews also died fighting in Gaza, a prominent campaign talking point.
The opposition also includes a joint ticket led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid, the secular nationalist party Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) led by former finance minister Avigdor Lieberman, and the Democrats led by former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan.
The Democrats party on Tuesday said Golan had been “approached in a threatening manner” by a man who was found to be carrying a knife. The lawmaker was attending a voting-day mobilization tour in Tel Aviv's HaMesila Park at the time of the incident.
"Golan’s security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground," the party said in a statement shared with the Guardian. "Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect." Golan, in his own statement, vowed that "incitement and violence will not deter us" and encouraged people to go out and vote.
Meanwhile, some polls had suggested that Eisenkot’s Yashar party may garner slightly more support than Netanyahu’s Likud, but they also projected that neither the Prime Minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition were likely to win the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government.
Including Arab parties such as United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List, or fringe parties, could be necessary to form a government. Both pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu coalitions have so far ruled out teaming up with the Arab-led parties. Arab citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population, though they receive fewer government services and endure higher poverty and unemployment rates. Discrimination and disappointment have historically depressed Arab-Israeli voter turnout. However, on Tuesday, there appeared to be strong turnout in some of Israel’s largest Arab-majority towns.
Netanyahu touts Trump endorsement
Netanyahu has brought attention to the support he received from his longstanding ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, who only announced his endorsement days before the election as conflict in the Middle East has tested their friendship.
In a late-night TV appearance on Oct. 25, Netanyahu boasted of Trump’s endorsement and said that Trump was willing to take action “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat” so long as Netanyahu stayed in power. Netanyahu added that he has already instructed Israel’s national intelligence agency Mossad as well as the IDF to “bring down” the Iranian regime. Trump remains very popular in Israel.
By contrast, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu for re-election, just a day after Trump put his “complete and total” support behind the Israeli leader.
“The President has the most effective endorsement in American, or international, political history,” said Vance, when asked in an interview if he would also be extending an endorsement of his own. “I endorse American candidates and that’s where I'm focused on, is the midterms, so I'm not getting involved in the Israeli elections.”
When pushed for an answer, Vance added: “I'm not anti-endorsing [Netanyahu], I'm not pro-endorsing him.”
A high-stakes election for Netanyahu
At stake for Netanyahu could be more than his continued leadership. The premier faces an international arrest warrant for alleged crimes related to the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. And even domestically, critics have demanded an inquiry into Netanyahu’s decision-making around Oct. 7. The attack, which resulted in over 1,200 people in Israel killed and around 250 hostages taken, is considered by many to be indicative of a major security failure.
The Gaza health ministry reports that since Oct. 7, 2023, more than 74,000 individuals have been killed. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, Gaza’s health ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME.
Another issue driving the election is public fury over ultra-Orthodox communities’ exemption from military conscription for men engaged in religious studies. Despite a shortage of soldiers, less than 10% of eligible ultra-Orthodox men enlist, amid demands from Netanyahu’s allies to exempt them. Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, has promised to end the de facto exemptions.
Netanyahu’s repeated attempts to reform the judiciary have also factored into this election, with critics slamming his undermining of democratic institutions and connecting it to his legal interests. Netanyahu is in the middle of a yearslong corruption trial, which he and his allies—including Trump—have claimed is politically motivated. He sought, but didn’t receive, a presidential pardon from Herzog.
When will we know the results?
About 7.3 million Israeli citizens were eligible to vote on Tuesday. The election fills the Knesset’s 120 seats through proportional representation—which means parties, not personalities, are on these voters’ ballots.
After polling stations closed at 10 p.m. (4 p.m. EDT), local media broadcasted initial exit polls. The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30, with official results published on Nov. 4.
But getting a clear picture of the Israeli government is likely to take longer.
No single party has ever claimed 61 seats to form a government, meaning Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Such alliances can take weeks or months to form, and what those coalitions may look like will depend on the election outcomes for smaller parties, which each need 3.25% of the votes to secure a seat in the Knesset.
Once the election winners are determined, President Herzog will refer to party leaders to choose a preferred Prime Minister and will ask the strongest candidate to form a government within 42 days. If a coalition cannot be formed after multiple attempts, the current Likud-led coalition government will continue to serve as caretaker before another round of elections is held in the coming months.

articles.title: Trump Administration Weighs Lifting Sanctions on Kremlin’s Investment Fund – NYT
articles.body:
The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), on which the former Biden administration imposed sanctions in the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russian officials pushed for the move during discussions on RDIF’s role in Russian diesel exports to the US, The New York Times reported on Tuesday, Oct. 27, citing people familiar with the matter. An unnamed US official confirmed to the newspaper that the US Treasury Department was reviewing the fund’s application for delisting through its standard procedures.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“While officially a sovereign wealth fund, RDIF is widely considered a slush fund for President Vladimir Putin and is emblematic of Russia’s broader kleptocracy,” the Treasury said under the former Biden administration.
By contrast, the US official told NYT that the current review was a part of an effort to improve bilateral relations between Moscow and Washington, with the fund’s chief executive, Kirill Dmitriev, praised as a “helpful envoy” in ending the war.
RDIF was initially created in 2011, by the order of former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev and then-Prime Minister, current Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Diesel deal paves way for sanctions relief
The request is linked to the diesel arrangement that Trump abruptly struck with Putin on Oct. 9, at the same time the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami, hoping to reach a breakthrough in Russia’s war.
‘Trump Is Cooked’: How Trump’s Russia Policy Is Splintering Republicans Ahead of the Midterms
Shortly after the deal’s announcement, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The move came only three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, appearing to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as networks close to Putin.
According to NYT, RDIF offered to handle transactions between Russian sellers and American buyers, while at the same time pushing for its removal from the sanctions list. To be delisted, RDIF would have to prove that the reasons for its original designation no longer apply.
Russian officials said three diesel tankers have sailed for the US this month, while Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct. 23 that RDIF had provided significant support for the shipments.
Some of the fuel left Russia before any US buyer had paid for it, people familiar with the matter told NYT.
Ship-tracking firms Kpler and TankerTrackers.com showed that one tanker, the Agioi Fanendes, departed the port of Primorsk on Oct. 23 and is expected in the US on Nov. 7.
It has since changed its listed destination from New York to “for orders,” meaning it has no discharge instructions yet.
From slush fund to trusted mediator
Eric Green, who oversaw Russia policy at the National Security Council under former President Joe Biden, told the NYT that lifting the sanctions would signal that Washington was abandoning its earlier position of keeping economic pressure on Moscow until a peace settlement was reached in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Dmitriev has become Moscow’s main economic channel to Trump’s team, working directly with senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
On Oct. 21, Witkoff publicly confirmed that Washington and Moscow are discussing future economic and trade cooperation, alongside negotiations to end the war.
He also revealed that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Dmitriev.
On that same day, Moscow revealed that Russia and the US are discussing the future of sanctioned Russian oil giant Lukoil’s overseas assets, valued at approximately $22 billion.
The US also proposed restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe, including reviving the Nord Stream pipeline system, The Economist reported on Oct. 22.
Earlier on Tuesday, Le Monde reported that the Kremlin is courting Trump and his inner circle with economic deals, including those in energy, civil aviation, rare earth metals and artificial intelligence (AI), without first agreeing to a ceasefire.
According to the same report, Witkoff presented Ukrainian negotiators in Florida on Oct. 9 with a postwar “regional prosperity plan,” which envisaged fully restoring Russian oil and gas supplies to Europe through Ukrainian territory.
Weeks of escalation triggered by diesel arrangement
The diesel agreement triggered weeks of severe diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
Around the same time, Trump claimed it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, while, days later, restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite network, disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Elon Musk claimed such limits were ultimately decided by Trump, not his company; a claim the US president denied.
On Oct. 14, in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan, President Volodymyr Zelensky described Trump’s diesel deal as a victory for Putin, warning that Moscow was exploiting Washington’s decisions to pressure Ukraine into concessions.
Around the time, Zelensky also suggested that Russia was offering Washington potential business ventures and economic projects to influence its decisions.
