articles.title: Alexander Solzhenitsyn warned against a war between Russians and Ukrainians. He also wanted to redraw Ukraine’s borders.
articles.body:
On October 20, a monument to Alexander Solzhenitsyn was dismantled in central Vladivostok, where it had stood since 2015. It was supposed to be moved to a park commemorating victims of political repression, but the very next day it was unexpectedly put back. The official explanation was that it was too large for the new site. Vladivostok’s role in this story is no coincidence. It was there that Solzhenitsyn began his journey across Russia in 1994, after 20 years in exile. The writer traveled across the country to Moscow by train. After returning, he became active in politics, criticizing Gorbachev and Yeltsin but speaking favorably of Putin. The feeling is mutual: Putin honors Solzhenitsyn’s memory despite the writer’s views on the USSR and its suppression of dissent. At Meduza’s request, historian Alexey Uvarov explains how Solzhenitsyn’s contradictory views took shape — and how they foreshadowed the Russian-Ukrainian war.
From Kislovodsk to Vermont: How Solzhenitsyn survived war and the camps and ended up in exile
Alexander Solzhenitsyn was born in Kislovodsk in 1918. His father died before he was born, and his mother raised him alone in Rostov-on-Don. The family was poor, but Solzhenitsyn developed a love of literature as a child. While still in school, he dreamed of writing a novel about the 1917 revolution. Like many of his peers, he sincerely believed in communism and saw the revolution as the first step toward building a just society. In 1936, Solzhenitsyn enrolled in the physics and mathematics department at Rostov University. He continued to dream of a writing career.
Solzhenitsyn was drafted into the army in 1941. After artillery school, he was sent to the front, where he commanded a sound-ranging battery, rose to the rank of captain, and received two military decorations. During the war, however, he began to question Joseph Stalin’s policies. Solzhenitsyn had not yet rejected communism itself. He believed Stalin had distorted Lenin’s ideas and that the Soviet system needed to return to its original principles. He discussed these thoughts in letters to his school friend Nikolai Vitkevich. Military censors read the letters, and in February 1945 Solzhenitsyn was arrested at the front. In July, the Special Council of the NKVD, the Soviet internal affairs agency, sentenced him to eight years in labor camps on charges of anti-Soviet agitation and attempting to establish an anti-Soviet organization.
Solzhenitsyn’s views gradually changed in prison. In conversations with other prisoners, he encountered criticism of Marxism itself as well as of Stalin. In time, the writer concluded that repression was inherent in the Soviet system, rather than simply a consequence of Stalin’s mistakes. He abandoned communism and returned to the Christian faith in which he had been raised. Solzhenitsyn spent part of his sentence in a “sharashka,” a secret research institute staffed by prisoners, and the final three years in a camp for political prisoners in Ekibastuz, Kazakhstan. After his release in 1953, he was sent into indefinite internal exile in Kazakhstan. Only in 1956 was Solzhenitsyn able to return to the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic; a year later, his conviction was overturned and his name cleared. He settled in Ryazan, took a job as a schoolteacher, and continued writing.
The Soviet “Thaw” gave him an opportunity to publish his work. In 1962, Alexander Tvardovsky, editor in chief of the journal Novy Mir, secured Nikita Khrushchev’s personal permission to publish Solzhenitsyn’s novella “Odin den Ivana Denisovicha” (“One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich”). The work attracted enormous interest and immediately made its author famous. But while the Soviet leadership was prepared to condemn Stalin’s crimes, it would not condemn the system of party dictatorship itself. After Khrushchev’s removal in 1964, Solzhenitsyn’s works were gradually barred from publication.
The writer had no intention of renouncing his work. In 1967, he openly challenged censorship, while his novel “V kruge pervom” (“In the First Circle”) and novella “Rakovy korpus” (“Cancer Ward”) circulated in samizdat — clandestinely copied editions — and were published abroad. In 1969, Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the Writers’ Union. A year later, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
His conflict with the authorities culminated in the publication of “Arkhipelag GULAG” (“The Gulag Archipelago”), which Solzhenitsyn had worked on in secret for many years. Drawing on his own experiences and the testimony of hundreds of former prisoners, he showed that mass repression had begun under Lenin and was rooted in the very nature of the Soviet state. The first volume was published in Paris in December 1973. By then, Solzhenitsyn was offering his own vision of the country’s future as well as criticizing its rulers.
That same year, he sent the Soviet leadership his “Pismo vozhdyam Sovetskogo Soyuza” (“Letter to the Soviet Leaders”), calling on them to abandon communist ideology and concentrate on domestic problems. The writer did not, however, advocate a transition to Western liberal democracy and was open to retaining authoritarian rule. In February 1974, Solzhenitsyn was arrested, stripped of his Soviet citizenship, and expelled to West Germany. He later moved to Switzerland, then to the United States in 1976.
The Vermont recluse: How Solzhenitsyn became a critic of both the USSR and the West
In 1976, Solzhenitsyn settled with his wife and children in the small town of Cavendish, Vermont. He bought a house surrounded by woods, where he could work away from journalists and public attention. His main project was the historical epic “Krasnoye Koleso” (“The Red Wheel”), which he had conceived in his youth. In it, the writer sought to understand the causes of the 1917 revolution and the Bolsheviks’ rise to power. He studied archival documents and eyewitness accounts, then spent months working on the manuscript.
Solzhenitsyn also maintained his ties to the USSR. After the publication of “The Gulag Archipelago,” he had established a fund to help Soviet political prisoners and their families, donating royalties from the book’s sales. Human rights activists secretly distributed the money inside the country. In 1977, Alexander Ginzburg, one of the fund’s leaders, was arrested, but the organization continued its work. Solzhenitsyn also collected Russian émigrés’ recollections to preserve accounts of the revolution, wars, and Soviet repression.
Although the writer rarely appeared in public, he continued to make political statements. His views differed markedly from those of many other critics of the USSR. Solzhenitsyn considered communism a destructive ideology, but he did not see Western society as a model for Russia’s future. This became particularly clear in June 1978, when he addressed Harvard University’s graduating class. Instead of praising American democracy, the writer criticized Western materialism, the excessive emphasis on individual rights, the influence of the press, and politicians’ unwillingness to confront communist regimes. The speech prompted debate in the press: Many critics accused Solzhenitsyn of ingratitude toward the country that had given him refuge and of rejecting liberal democracy.
Solzhenitsyn also clashed with other émigrés from the USSR. His dispute with the writer Andrei Sinyavsky was particularly bitter. In “Nashi plyuralisty” (“Our Pluralists”), an article published in 1983, Solzhenitsyn accused some émigré intellectuals of having collaborated with the Soviet authorities and now claiming the right to determine Russia’s future. His opponents, in turn, criticized his Russian nationalism and authoritarian views.
Christianity was central to Solzhenitsyn’s worldview. In May 1983, he received the Templeton Prize for his contribution to religious thought. Speaking in London to mark the award, the writer said that society’s abandonment of faith in God was the main cause of Russia’s 20th-century tragedies. He saw this loss of faith as the source of both Soviet totalitarianism and the moral crisis in Western society.
In 1985, Solzhenitsyn remained one of the world’s best-known Russian writers, but his works were still not being published in his homeland. The possibility of returning to Russia seemed remote.
Perestroika and the return to Russia: How Solzhenitsyn planned the country’s future from exile
Mikhail Gorbachev’s rise to power in 1985 changed conditions in the USSR. His policies of perestroika and glasnost allowed previously forbidden subjects, including Stalinist repression, to be discussed openly. The authorities were in no hurry to allow Solzhenitsyn’s works back into print, however. In 1987, Novy Mir editor in chief Sergei Zalygin said the journal planned to publish “Cancer Ward,” and the following year he approached the writer himself. But Solzhenitsyn set a condition: “The Gulag Archipelago” had to be published in the USSR first. He believed readers needed access to this book about the Soviet system’s crimes before any of his other works.
In 1989, Novy Mir finally began publishing chapters of “The Gulag Archipelago.” Other works by the writer soon began appearing in the USSR, and he again became a subject of public debate. In August 1990, Gorbachev restored Solzhenitsyn’s citizenship and that of his wife. The writer was not yet planning to return, however. He wanted to finish “The Red Wheel” and secure the formal dismissal of the treason charge brought against him before his expulsion in 1974.
Solzhenitsyn was already taking an active part in discussions about the country’s future. In September 1990, Komsomolskaya Pravda and Literaturnaya Gazeta published his article “Kak nam obustroit Rossiyu?” (“Rebuilding Russia: Reflections and Tentative Proposals”), with a print run of nearly 27 million copies.
The writer took it as a given that the communist system was doomed and proposed his own plan for transforming the state. He called for abandoning imperial ambitions and not using force to hold on to republics seeking independence.
At the same time, Solzhenitsyn advocated preserving a union of Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Kazakhstan. He also proposed redrawing some republics’ borders because he considered parts of their territory historically Russian. The writer envisioned Russia as a state with strong local self-government, grounded in national and Christian traditions rather than Western political models.
The article provoked fierce debate. Many welcomed the call to abandon communism and focus on domestic problems. But the proposals concerning Ukraine’s and Kazakhstan’s borders drew sharp criticism. Gorbachev also rejected the plan, considering Solzhenitsyn’s views too conservative. Events moved faster than the writer had anticipated. In December 1991, the USSR collapsed, and his proposed union never materialized.
By then, the legal barriers to Solzhenitsyn’s return had also been removed. In September 1991, the Soviet Prosecutor General’s Office dismissed the case against him, finding that his actions did not constitute a crime. But the writer remained in Vermont for almost another three years. He continued working on his books and following Russian politics. Solzhenitsyn welcomed the fall of the communist regime, but Boris Yeltsin’s economic reforms and the population’s impoverishment left him increasingly disillusioned.
On May 27, 1994, 20 years after his expulsion, Solzhenitsyn finally returned to Russia with his wife and son. He deliberately chose a route through the Far East so that he could cross the country by train and see how it had changed. His plane landed first in Magadan, then in Vladivostok. From there, the writer traveled west by rail, arriving in Moscow on July 21.
From support to disillusionment: How Solzhenitsyn became an unyielding opponent of Yeltsin
After returning to Russia, Solzhenitsyn had no intention of confining himself to literature. Over his 20 years in exile, he had developed his own vision of how the country should be organized after communism, and now he wanted to join the debate over its future. But what he saw on his journey across Russia disappointed him. The writer spoke of poverty, corruption, and a privatization process that had put state property into the hands of a small group of people. He called the political system a “sham democracy” and “an ingenious fusion of bureaucrats, Soviet party officials, and hardened wheeler-dealers.”
The Kremlin initially counted on his support. Solzhenitsyn’s biographer Lyudmila Saraskina writes that Yeltsin was certain the writer would be “on our side.” Reformers saw him as an ally against communism, but his criticism of the economic changes increasingly echoed the rhetoric of the communist opposition. The liberal press began calling Solzhenitsyn “the choirmaster of the doomsayers.”
Solzhenitsyn laid out his views most fully in a speech to the State Duma on October 28, 1994. Lawmakers had spent several months debating whether to invite the writer, with the pro-presidential Russia’s Choice faction voting against it. Solzhenitsyn spoke for about an hour. He said Russia had “no democracy, only oligarchy” — rule by “a small, closed circle of people.” He proposed developing local self-government along the lines of the prerevolutionary zemstvos, elected bodies responsible for schools, hospitals, and roads. The writer did not oppose a strong presidency and believed it should be preserved, but he thought its powers should be increasingly limited at lower levels of government, with residents making their own decisions at the local level. Solzhenitsyn also expressed mixed views on the idea of having the president appoint regional leaders. He warned lawmakers that parliament risked sharing the fate of the prerevolutionary Dumas if it could not stand up to the executive branch.
Lawmakers gave the speech a cool reception: No one asked questions, and the applause was tepid. The writer’s supporters saw this as evidence of politicians’ indifference to the country’s troubles. Reformers, meanwhile, considered Solzhenitsyn’s proposals outdated. Yegor Gaidar said with regret that the speech had pleased the communists.
His relationship with Yeltsin was also difficult. In August 1991, Solzhenitsyn welcomed Yeltsin’s resistance to the State Committee for the State of Emergency, which had attempted a coup, but soon began criticizing his economic policies. In June 1992, they spoke by phone for 40 minutes, and the writer said he had “failed to convince him of anything.” The president also publicly challenged his prominent critic. In “Zapiski prezidenta” (“The Struggle for Russia”), he responded to Solzhenitsyn’s question about whether he would treat his own mother with shock therapy: “I would use shock therapy on myself, and not just one time.”
On November 16, 1994, they met in person, with their wives and without journalists. Yeltsin’s press secretary, Vyacheslav Kostikov, recalled that the president was nervous and that his advisers had tried to talk him out of the meeting. The conversation lasted about four hours and, in Kostikov’s words, proceeded “without glossing over political differences.” Solzhenitsyn recounted his journey across the country and outlined his proposals. But no noticeable changes in government policy followed.
Another source of disagreement soon emerged. In December 1994, Russian troops entered Chechnya, which had effectively been outside Moscow’s control since 1991. Solzhenitsyn considered the decision to go to war a “grave political mistake.” In 1992, he had advised Yeltsin to let Chechnya go if it wanted to secede. Later, the writer proposed recognizing the republic’s independence, but separating it from Russia with a line of military posts along the border and retaining the territory on the left bank of the Terek River as part of Russia. In 2000, after Chechen militants invaded Dagestan, he acknowledged that his earlier advice to Yeltsin had been a mistake.
Solzhenitsyn also tried to reach television audiences. Beginning in April 1995, his 15-minute addresses aired on ORT every two weeks. He spoke about schools, the army, elections, the situation of Russians outside Russia, and the war in Chechnya. But the program was canceled after 12 episodes. The 13th episode, devoted to people’s disillusionment with politics and criticism of the authorities, never aired. “They’ve shut me up, just as I expected,” Solzhenitsyn said. ORT’s management said it had made the decision because of the approaching parliamentary elections and the need to maintain political balance. But because other critical programs were taken off the air at the same time, the decision prompted suspicions of political censorship. Solzhenitsyn no longer had a regular television audience, though he continued to travel around the country and express his views in the press.
By the late 1990s, his criticism of Yeltsin had grown even harsher. In May 1998, he published “Rossiya v obvale” (“Russia in Collapse”). In it, Solzhenitsyn accused the authorities of carrying out unfair privatization, destroying industry and science, impoverishing the population, and giving in to the West. He did not call for a return to the Soviet system, but he considered the existing political order unacceptable. The book appeared three months before the August debt default, which gave his criticism added weight.
His differences with Yeltsin came to a head in December 1998. To mark the writer’s 80th birthday, the president awarded him the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle, Russia’s highest state honor. Solzhenitsyn had sent the presidential administration a written refusal in advance, but Yeltsin signed the decree anyway. On December 11, his birthday, at the premiere of Yury Lyubimov’s play “Sharashka” (“The Prison Research Institute”) at the Taganka Theater, he said from the stage: “I cannot accept an award from the country’s highest authority, which has brought Russia to its present disastrous state.” The writer did, however, accept Yeltsin’s personal birthday greetings.
Putin and Solzhenitsyn: How a dissident and a KGB officer grew close
Solzhenitsyn entered 2000 as an unyielding critic of Yeltsin. He reacted sharply to Yeltsin’s resignation and acting President Putin’s decree granting the former head of state immunity. Speaking at the Russian State Library in May 2000, he said: “I consider it disgraceful to absolve Yeltsin of responsibility. And probably not just Yeltsin — another hundred or two should stand trial along with him!”
Solzhenitsyn was initially wary of the country’s new leadership as well. In interviews with NTV and Novaya Gazeta, he criticized Putin’s intention to continue Yeltsin’s reforms: “So far, we have seen no encouraging steps from the new authorities to put things right.”
Within a few months, however, his attitude toward the new president had become noticeably more favorable. On September 20, 2000, Putin and his wife visited Solzhenitsyn at his country home in Troitse-Lykovo. The following day, the writer said the president had made a good impression on him. He praised Putin’s quick mind and described his decisions as “prudent and sound,” saying Putin had “no thirst for personal power.” Solzhenitsyn said the two did not always agree, but listened carefully to each other’s arguments.
The meeting provoked debate. To many former Soviet dissidents, the growing closeness between the author of “The Gulag Archipelago” and a former KGB officer seemed paradoxical. Andrei Sakharov’s widow, Yelena Bonner, wondered how “the regime’s most fearless opponent became friends with a KGB colonel.”
Still, Solzhenitsyn’s approval of the president did not mean he stopped criticizing the authorities. In December 2000, while accepting an award from the French Academy of Moral and Political Sciences, he sharply criticized the political elite, which he believed was dominated by “unrepentant members of the old nomenclatura” and “rapacious former heads of the Komsomol.” Answering journalists’ questions after the ceremony, the writer recounted what he had told Putin at their private meeting: “Strengthening the state is necessary for Russia’s unity, but strengthening the state will not make Russia flourish. Russia can flourish only when millions are free to speak, when they are free in word and deed to shape their own destiny.”
Solzhenitsyn and Putin agreed above all on the need to strengthen the state. The writer believed that the collapse of the USSR and the economic upheavals of the 1990s had left Russia in a deep crisis, and that the new president was trying to rebuild the state.
In a July 2007 interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel, Solzhenitsyn said Putin had inherited a country that had been “ransacked and knocked off its feet” and had begun gradually rebuilding it. The writer also said he was “dismayed” by the slow development of local self-government and regretted the absence of a sizable, constructive political opposition in Russia. In the same interview, he called Putin’s decision to abolish elections to the State Duma in single-member districts a mistake.
In private conversations, Solzhenitsyn could be even more explicit in criticizing Putin’s decisions. In April 2008, a few months before his death, he met with U.S. Ambassador William Burns. According to a diplomatic cable published later, the writer called the abolition of gubernatorial elections a “mistake.” He said citizens should be able to choose their own representatives in government and hold them accountable. As an example, Solzhenitsyn recalled town meetings in Vermont, which he called the very essence of democracy.
Putin and Solzhenitsyn also had similar views on relations with the West. Solzhenitsyn had long criticized Western policy, but his judgments became even harsher after NATO’s bombing of Yugoslavia in 1999. In a 2006 interview with Moskovskiye Novosti, he said NATO’s expansion was intended to encircle Russia and strip it of its sovereignty. A year later, the writer called Putin’s foreign policy “quite reasonable and more foresighted,” while criticizing NATO’s efforts to bring former Soviet republics, particularly Ukraine, into its orbit.
The Russian State Prize, awarded to Solzhenitsyn in 2007 “for outstanding achievements in humanitarian work,” symbolized the closeness between the writer and the president. Solzhenitsyn had refused the Order of St. Andrew from Yeltsin in 1998, but accepted Putin’s award. He explained his decision by noting that the prize had been awarded by a panel of experts rather than by the president personally. In his Der Spiegel interview, Solzhenitsyn also answered a question about Putin’s past: “Vladimir Putin — yes, he was an officer of the intelligence services, but he was not a KGB investigator, nor was he the head of a camp in the gulag.”
On June 12, 2007, the writer’s wife, Natalia, accepted the award at the Kremlin. Solzhenitsyn himself was unable to attend because of his health. After the ceremony, Putin visited him at home for another conversation. The president told journalists that many of the authorities’ actions were in keeping with Solzhenitsyn’s ideas.
Life after death: How the authorities put Solzhenitsyn’s legacy to work for them
Solzhenitsyn died on August 3, 2008, at 89. By then, Putin had become prime minister, and Dmitry Medvedev was president. Both paid their respects to the writer: Putin attended the public memorial service, and Medvedev the funeral at the Donskoy Monastery. On the day of the funeral, Medvedev signed a decree commemorating Solzhenitsyn. Scholarships were established in his honor, and Moscow’s Bolshaya Kommunisticheskaya Street was soon renamed Alexander Solzhenitsyn Street, despite protests from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation. Later, an abridged version of “The Gulag Archipelago,” prepared with the involvement of the writer’s widow, Natalia, was produced for schoolchildren.
The Russian authorities continued to honor Solzhenitsyn’s memory in the years that followed. In December 2018, to mark the centenary of the writer’s birth, Putin personally unveiled a monument to him in Moscow. In his speech, the president called Solzhenitsyn a “true patriot” who, even in exile, “opposed any manifestations of Russophobia.” In this way, Solzhenitsyn’s devotion to Russia and defense of its national interests — not just his fight against Soviet repression — took on special prominence in the official portrayal of the writer.
The writer’s widow, Natalia Solzhenitsyna, plays an important role in preserving and interpreting his legacy. In a 2018 interview with the French newspaper Le Figaro, she supported the annexation of Crimea, calling it a restoration of historical justice. Solzhenitsyna also acknowledged that the peninsula’s annexation was contentious under international law and opposed Russian intervention in the Donbas. She said the intervention was an enormous mistake that the country would come to regret.
In 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the publisher AST released “S Ukrainoy budet chrezvychayno bolno” (“Ukraine Will Be an Extremely Painful Problem”), a collection compiled by Solzhenitsyna. The book continued a project begun in 2018 with the collection “Rossiya. Zapad. Ukraina” (“Russia. The West. Ukraine”). It brought together Solzhenitsyn’s statements on Russian-Ukrainian relations, disputed territories, and Western policy. In the foreword, the writer’s widow repeated her husband’s arguments about the injustice of Ukraine’s Soviet-era borders and Western countries’ responsibility for the deterioration in relations between Russia and Ukraine.
Yet in May 2022, Natalia Solzhenitsyna also signed a written pledge vouching for opposition politician Vladimir Kara-Murza, who had been arrested on charges of spreading “fake news” about the Russian army.
Solzhenitsyn, Ukraine, and Kazakhstan: How the writer’s views grew more radical
Solzhenitsyn’s views provoked particularly fierce debate in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. The writer recognized peoples’ right to self-determination and opposed forcibly keeping republics within a common state. Yet he considered large parts of Ukrainian and Kazakhstani territory historically Russian. This contradiction persisted in his statements for decades.
Solzhenitsyn’s early reflections on Ukraine seemed fairly conciliatory. In “The Gulag Archipelago,” the bulk of which he finished writing in 1968, the writer recalled his conversations with Ukrainian nationalists in Soviet camps. He criticized the authorities’ habit of labeling them bandits and considered Ukrainians’ desire for independence understandable.
Despite their shared history, Russians and Ukrainians had failed over several centuries to learn to live in harmony, Solzhenitsyn acknowledged. “Ukraine will be an extremely painful problem,” he warned. But he considered it unacceptable to hold on to Ukraine by force. Ukrainians themselves, he believed, should decide their country’s future. The writer nevertheless hoped that a peaceful separation would eventually allow the two peoples to reunite.
In May 1975, Solzhenitsyn recorded an Easter radio address to Ukrainians in Canada. In it, he recalled his own Ukrainian roots: His mother was almost entirely of Ukrainian descent, and his maternal grandfather spoke Ukrainian. The writer said he did not speak Ukrainian fluently but understood it well. He recalled Ukrainians’ suffering, including the famine of the 1930s, and his friendships with Ukrainian prisoners in Soviet camps. Polish historian Grzegorz Przebinda of Jagiellonian University said the address was included in neither the 2018 collection “Russia. The West. Ukraine” nor the 2022 volume “Ukraine Will Be an Extremely Painful Problem,” both prepared by the writer’s widow.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
Even during this period, however, Solzhenitsyn’s attitude toward Ukraine was becoming more contradictory. Przebinda found that, when preparing a new edition of “The Gulag Archipelago” in 1980, the writer added a remark to his earlier reflections saying that Khrushchev had arbitrarily transferred Crimea to Ukraine. At the same time, some sympathetic statements about the Ukrainian national movement disappeared from the book.
Solzhenitsyn nevertheless continued to oppose violence between the two peoples. In 1981, he sent a letter to the organizers of a conference on Russian-Ukrainian relations in Toronto. In it, the writer urged that no one be held by force and promised that “never, under any circumstances, shall I take part in a Russian-Ukrainian clash or allow my sons to do so.”
By the early 1990s, territorial claims were becoming increasingly prominent in his thinking. In “Rebuilding Russia,” Solzhenitsyn proposed letting most Soviet republics go while preserving a union of Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Kazakhstan. He denied that a distinct Ukrainian people had existed since the early Middle Ages, calling such ideas “a recently invented falsehood.” The writer also maintained that the Kherson region, the area around the Sea of Azov, Crimea, and the Donbas had never been part of historical Ukraine. He considered Kazakhstan’s territory an artificial creation of the Soviet authorities and proposed keeping its northern regions within Russia. Solzhenitsyn still recognized Ukrainians’ and Kazakhs’ right to independence in principle, but he believed that each region should decide separately which state it would belong to.
These proposals provoked a sharp reaction. In September 1990, participants in a rally in Alma-Ata against Solzhenitsyn’s territorial claims publicly burned a newspaper containing his article. The Lviv Regional Council also condemned the writer’s statements. His critics included former Ukrainian political prisoners who, like Solzhenitsyn himself, had endured the Soviet camps.
In August 1991, before the Soviet Union collapsed, Solzhenitsyn called on Yeltsin to reconsider the Soviet republics’ borders. He asked the president to ensure that votes in Ukraine’s forthcoming independence referendum would be counted separately in each region. In the writer’s view, residents should decide for themselves which state their territories belonged to. In a 1994 interview with Forbes, he again said he wished Ukraine success, but only within borders that he himself considered ethnically justified.
In his final years, Solzhenitsyn’s views on Ukrainian politics hardened further. In 2006, he called the alleged suppression of the Russian language in Ukraine “an act of atrocity” and again questioned Ukraine’s right to Crimea and its eastern regions. In April 2008, four months before his death, he published an article in Izvestia titled “Possorit rodnye narody?” (“Swallowing Shameless Lies”). The writer opposed recognizing the famine of 1932–1933 as a genocide of Ukrainians and compared the Ukrainian authorities’ arguments to Bolshevik propaganda.
The article outraged former Ukrainian political prisoners. Levko Lukyanenko and other human rights advocates called on Russian intellectuals not to support this interpretation of the Holodomor. They also expressed hope that Solzhenitsyn himself would find the courage to “live not by lies” — a reference to his own 1974 essay, “Zhit ne po lzhi” (“Live Not by Lies”).
How to view Solzhenitsyn in 2026
It would be wrong to reduce Solzhenitsyn either to his “great-power” views or to his condemnation of Soviet camps and repression. He was a complex person whose political convictions changed throughout his life. Though he did not support Western liberal democracy, the writer defended freedom of speech, human dignity, and local self-government.
But in today’s Russia, the “great-power” side of his legacy has come to the fore. Putin found ideas that matched his own views in the writer’s reflections on a strong state and national interests. As a result, Solzhenitsyn, who remains unacceptable to many admirers of the Soviet past, has gained a prominent place in the state’s efforts to shape historical memory.
Other parts of his legacy, meanwhile, increasingly conflict with the Russian authorities’ actions. Even as the state honors the author of “The Gulag Archipelago,” a Moscow museum devoted to Soviet repression has been closed and replaced by a museum of victims of Nazi crimes.
Still more striking is the contradiction with the principle of “protecting the people,” which Solzhenitsyn considered one of the state’s main responsibilities and which Putin himself quoted in 2006. The war against Ukraine, with its enormous loss of life, is difficult to reconcile with that principle. In closing, all that remains is to quote Solzhenitsyn once more, from his essay “‘Russky vopros’ k kontsu XX veka” (“The ‘Russian Question’ at the End of the Twentieth Century”):
We do not need to be a world arbiter, to compete for international leadership (stronger volunteers will surface); all our efforts must be directed inwards, towards assiduous inner development.

articles.title: Germany’s Helsing Unveils Low-Cost Highspeed Drone Interceptors
articles.body:
Helsing, a German military AI company, unveiled its Contra AI-controlled autonomous air defense system via a video posted on X on Monday. Helsing described it as a cost-effective system optimized to tackle jet-powered drone and missile attacks.
Helsing’s Contra system is intended to solve the existing air defense conundrum where the only current way of effectively intercepting jet-powered drones such as Russia’s Geran 4s and 5s is the use of multimillion-dollar interceptors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Contra is intended to control two relatively inexpensive interceptor missiles: the AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush said to cost less than $100,000 each compared with Patriot PAC-3 missiles at $4-5 million a unit and the NASAMS (AMRAAM / AIM-9X) at around $1million a throw.
The military issues website Defense News cites recent intelligence reports, that Russia is increasing jet-powered drone and cruise missile production, to as much as 4,000 units a month, which, along with launch sites, could bring parts of the EU within range.
Artificial intelligence and interceptor speed, the key
While still at the developmental stage, Helsing bills Contra, based on its well-proven Altra C2 platform, as an autonomous AI-based operation that will allow the real-time detection and engagement of hundreds or more drone and missile threats into a single air defense picture.
It is anticipated to be “field-ready” by late 2027, with Helsing saying its seekers rely on European supply chains and is free from Chinese components.
Russia Says Three Tankers With Diesel En Route to US
Intercepts would be achieved through a combination of two, advanced radar guided, container-launched missile interceptors whose performance is designed to overlap and supplement each other’s capability.
The AD-1 “Inferno,” which Helsing Chief Executive Gundbert Scherf says is intended as the “workhorse” of the counter-drone system, is powered by a jet engine, and flies at around 700 kph (435 mph) at a range of around 20 kilometers (12 miles). It can loiter over a defended area, swarm with other interceptors, and make repeated passes.
The AD-2 “Ambush,” intended as a rapid interceptor against drones and missiles that break through the AD-1 “net,” has a solid rocket motor and is said to have a flight speed of Mach 2.5 (1,900 mph, 3,000 kph) at a range of in excess of 20 kilometers (12 miles).
Both systems are able to be redirected mid-course by the Contra ground stations with an onboard radar-seeker for all-weather terminal guidance. While designed for, and capable of, stand-alone operation, Helsing said the system is set up to rapidly integrate with third-party counter-drone systems including missile interceptors, lasers, and guns. The company said Contra has already demonstrated such hardware integrations to multiple military customers.
Niklas Köhler, Co-Founder and President of Helsing, says: “Contra ends the air defense dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometers (6+ miles) high – affordable and at industrial scale.”

articles.title: Air defenses neutralize two ballistic missiles, 255 drones in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Air defenses neutralize two ballistic missiles, 255 drones in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
Ukraine’s Air Force reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
Starting at 6 p.m. on Monday, October 26, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/S-400 missiles launched from Russia’s Bryansk region and 280 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones (69 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones. The drones were launched from Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, Shatalovo, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
Kyiv was the main target of the attack.
The air attack was countered by Ukrainian Defense Forces aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile air defense groups.
According to preliminary data, as of 9 a.m. on Tuesday, October 27, air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 257 targets: two ballistic missiles and 255 drones.
Hits were recorded at 25 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 16 locations.
Several attack drones remaine in the air, and air defense operations are ongoing.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian ballistic missile strikes carried out since the evening of October 26 affected six districts of Kyiv. A 46-year-old woman was killed, and 15 people were injured.
Source: Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine via Telegram

articles.title: Weighing dependence on Washington: Trump between Zelensky and Netanyahu
articles.body:
Within eight days in October, US President Donald Trump made two statements about two wartime leaders that, placed side by side, read like a confession. On 10 October, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, he said of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky: “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” He accused Zelensky of passing up the chance to settle the war with Russia “many times, many many times” and of driving up diesel prices by striking Russian oil refineries: “He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
On 18 October, Trump posted a letter on his Truth Social platform describing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace.” In the letter, he gave Netanyahu his “Complete and Total Endorsement” nine days before Israel’s general election on 27 October.
Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu was expected, given Washington’s long record of backing Israel. His remarks on Zelensky, by contrast, shocked many. They revealed the real logic of the Trump administration: politics driven by calculations of interest rather than by allegiances or alliances. Together, the two statements hold an important lesson for anyone who believes American support is a promise rather than a calculation. They also expose Zelensky’s own strategic failure: he relied on a foreign power with its own interests instead of honestly weighing his own capabilities in the conflict with Russia.
A card that no longer plays
Zelensky’s fall from grace was triggered by a dispute over diesel. On 9 October, after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced a deal under which Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and larger volumes after that. The Kremlin said Russia was ready to supply “the American and global markets.” Zelensky condemned the agreement as “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” and warned that Russia would “repay” the diesel “with further terror and perfidy.”
Trump responded with fury. For weeks, he had pressed Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian refineries, which had cut Russian diesel output and pushed up global fuel prices. A US official told Axios that Trump struck the deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored his requests. Driven by his own political calculations, Trump wanted Ukraine to stop unilaterally and made no matching demand of Moscow. “We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries,” Trump told reporters. “So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries.”
The domestic context was decisive. The US was just over three weeks away from the midterm elections on 3 November. Diesel prices were close to record highs, driving up the cost of almost everything. Trump’s approval rating had fallen to the lowest point of his presidency amid the war on Iran, which the US and Israel launched in February. That war, and to a lesser extent the Ukrainian drone strikes, lay behind the energy crisis. By blaming Zelensky, Trump sought to shift responsibility for rising prices onto a foreign leader at a moment when American voters were preparing to punish the party in power.
The episode shows that Zelensky’s abandonment is not tactical but structural. He is no longer a useful card in American domestic politics, where Ukraine has no lobby to match the influence of pro-Israel groups. The Trump administration, along with other Western political circles, appears to have concluded that the war against Russia cannot be won.
Behind Trump’s insult lie facts about this war that are hard to deny. Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 was an act of aggression in breach of international law. Yet even if Western countries encouraged Kyiv to keep fighting, the choice to pursue the conflict on the battlefield rather than at the negotiating table was ultimately Zelensky’s, and he bet everything on Western support. His former spokeswoman Yulia Mendel has claimed that he undermined around seven attempts to end the war, an allegation his office rejects as baseless. In October 2022, he also signed a decree declaring negotiations with Putin “impossible”. The result is plain: having relied heavily on foreign powers, he is now stuck in a quagmire, with foreign support shrinking and no prospect of gains on the battlefield.
A war criminal who remains indispensable
Netanyahu is a different calculation entirely. In November 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The warrant remains in force even though Washington has sanctioned the court’s judges and deputy prosecutors and its president. He is a fugitive from international justice. Yet a sitting American president has endorsed his re-election in the most personal terms available.
Why? Because Trump needs him, both for his war on Iran and for electoral calculations shaped by pro-Israel lobbying networks in American politics. The most prominent of these is the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which a US senator says plans to spend $233 million to defeat candidates critical of Netanyahu’s government. If Trump abandoned Netanyahu now, he would be abandoning his own decision to go to war with Iran. He believes the Israeli leader is central to the future of the US confrontation with Iran, and he does not want to carry on alone, which would become far more complicated if Netanyahu loses. Trump spelt this out himself: “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.” The endorsement was not moral; it rested on political calculation and self-interest.
The lesson: interest, not values
The contrast between Zelensky and Netanyahu is not one between good and bad. It is a practical lesson in how far a leader can rely on a foreign power. Netanyahu remains indispensable not because the case against him has gone away, but because he remains useful to the man who endorsed him. Zelensky was discarded because, at least in Trump’s view, he had become useless, with no domestic constituency in the US to protect him.
The difference is not between two leaders or their conflicts. It is between an asset and a liability. It is Zelensky’s own fault, not anyone else’s, that he failed to recognise the limits of American support when he chose to continue the war rather than settle it through direct talks. He believed a foreign leader would back him without exacting a price. Trump sees Netanyahu as an asset he would like to keep in power, while Zelensky was traded for a diesel deal that carries electoral value for Trump and his party in the upcoming midterms.
Return, finally, to the two men. One is a wanted war crimes suspect who received a presidential endorsement in a public letter. The other is a wartime president who was told publicly that his country should find someone else. The contrast is not an anomaly to be explained away; it is an instruction manual. Those who place their fate in Washington’s hands should study Zelensky’s path and adjust their expectations of a foreign power, whose support will never come at the expense of its own interests. That is American politics today.

articles.title: A Russian IT worker joined the army to ‘benefit society’ and was promised a job operating drones. Now he’s missing in Ukraine, and his wife believes his commanders stole his money.
articles.body:
A Russian IT worker joined the army to ‘benefit society’ and was promised a job operating drones. Now he’s missing in Ukraine, and his wife believes his commanders stole his money.
An IT specialist from Chelyabinsk signed a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry that promised him service in the drone forces. Instead, he ended up in what’s known as a “meat grinder regiment.” He was sent on an assault and went missing, his wife told the independent Russian investigative outlet iStories.
Nikolai and Irina (names changed) had been together for 20 years and raised two children. The family didn’t need money: Nikolai developed software for government agencies at a large IT company.
In the summer of 2026, Nikolai decided to go to war to “benefit society.” “When the special military operation started in the country, a lot of our friends left for abroad. We kind of looked down on that. I can’t explain it now. But still, we had a question: who’s going to defend the country then? Defend its interests?” Irina told journalists.
An appendix to the contract specified that Nikolai would serve as a drone operator and undergo training for that role. Instead, he was sent to military unit No. 95378 in the Samara region, home to the 1437th Motorized Rifle Regiment, where he spent several months. He received no training or weapons instruction at all, doing “housekeeping work” and serving as a “company clerk” instead.
Russia’s Defense Ministry has been actively recruiting Russians, including students, into the drone forces since late 2025. Recruiters promise high salaries, one-year contracts, and service far from the front line, but in reality, the contracts are open-ended, and recruiters cannot guarantee any special conditions of service.
In conversations with his wife, Nikolai said that his unit practiced extortion and harshly punished discipline violations: putting offenders in a pit or sending them on assaults.
In September, Nikolai called his wife and said he was being sent on a combat mission:
One day he called from someone else’s phone number and said he was being sent on a combat mission and wanted to say goodbye. At first I didn’t understand anything. I said, how is that possible? Were you even trained for anything? What mission are you being sent on? He said he didn’t know, and to be honest, he started crying. Then the call cut off.
Soon after, his wife received a notice from command that Nikolai had gone missing on September 28 “while performing tasks during the special military operation.” What exactly happened to him on the combat mission remains unknown.
Irina found a notification from the online marketplace Ozon in her husband’s email showing that Nikolai, while at the front, had bought five laptops for 120,000 rubles. She believes someone among his commanders stole about one and a half million rubles from his bank card. On social media, she found complaints about commanders from relatives of other servicemen who served in the same unit.
The 1437th Regiment, where Nikolai served, is part of the 15th Separate Guards Motorized Rifle Brigade. Its unofficial name is the “Black Hussars.” Before Russia’s full-scale war with Ukraine, it was the only “peacekeeping” brigade in the Russian army. Its soldiers carried out missions in Georgia and Nagorno-Karabakh and likely took part in the annexation of Crimea.
In the war against Ukraine, the brigade took part in the occupation of the Kyiv region. Brigade servicemen are suspected of torturing and killing civilians. The unit itself also practices torture and extrajudicial killings, the independent Russian news outlet Verstka reported.
The 1437th Regiment is commanded by Colonel Vladimir Teslo, 31, iStories found. In 2024, Vladimir Putin awarded him the title Hero of Russia “for the totality of heroic acts and personal courage.”
“On the one hand, the regiment commander is a Hero of Russia. On the other, that same commander sees his soldiers as walking wallets. First he empties their bank accounts, then he gets rid of the soldiers themselves. I want people to know about this Teslo. He may be a hero for one thing, but he’s a murderer for another. I don’t know what will come of speaking out. It’s too early to tell. These are deranged men with guns,” Irina told journalists.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts 2 Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh
articles.body:
Şahin Demir
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Tuesday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group toward the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki announced the interception in a post on the US social media platform X, without providing further details on possible casualties or damage.
Earlier Tuesday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province.
It also announced the interception and destruction of four drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom’s southern region.
The interceptions came amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition against the Houthis since March 2015, after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other parts of the country in 2014.

articles.title: German troops test Auterion’s Talon drone interceptor
articles.body:
- Auterion showed its Talon interceptor drone on a test range with the Bundeswehr, launched from a rifle-style launcher and guided by a second soldier.
- The company says Talon can engage single drones and swarms but did not disclose its performance or any German purchase plans.
Auterion, the drone software company best known for the autonomy systems inside thousands of Ukrainian strike drones, has shown its Talon interceptor on a test range with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, saying the system is built to take on both single drones and swarms.
Footage released by the company this week shows several German soldiers in Flecktarn camouflage working with the system on an open airfield, with one soldier firing the Talon interceptor drone into the air from a special rifle-style launcher fitted with an optical sight, while another soldier standing nearby guides the drone onto its target after launch.
Auterion did not say where or when the trials took place, which Bundeswehr unit was involved, or whether Talon destroyed any targets during the tests, and the company has given few technical details about the interceptor itself.
In the way it is used, Talon resembles Russia’s Yolka, a small interceptor drone that Russian troops fire from a handheld launcher at an aerial target that has already been spotted, and which uses an optical seeker and an onboard AI module to track its target out to about 3 km (1.9 miles) at speeds of up to 200 km/h (124 mph), although Yolka is described as a largely fire-and-forget weapon, while the Talon footage shows a second soldier steering the drone after launch.
Auterion’s chief executive, Lorenz Meier, described the company’s approach to interceptors in July, saying the first version would be simple enough for a soldier to point the interceptor at an identified target and launch it, with later versions moving into vehicle launchers, deeper integration with air defense networks and fixed installations to protect sites such as airports, stadiums and government buildings.
The company, which has a major hub in Munich, has been growing its business in Germany through a joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Airlogix that was formed in February 2026 with backing from the German and Ukrainian governments, and the venture began serial production in September of more than 5,000 Seth X and Anubis strike drones under a German government-funded contract, using Auterion software for AI-guided terminal navigation and flight without satellite navigation.
Germany is buying several layers of counter-drone defense at once, and in November 2025 the Bundestag’s budget committee approved about €490 million (about $546 million) for MBDA’s DefendAir short-range anti-drone missile, while the Bundeswehr has also signed contracts for interceptor drones with other companies, such as TYTAN Technologies.

articles.title: Houthis claim to have hit Saudi Ras Tanura oil refinery, defense ministry with ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile.
The Houthis also said they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route.
Intensifying hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have further disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began.
The Houthis' military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on the Ras Tanura refinery had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and is located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz.
Saree also claimed that the Houthis had hit the Saudi Ministry of Defense with a ballistic missile and Abha International Airport with a drone.
Saudi authorities did not confirm any of the strikes.
Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure.
Nearly all Saudi Arabia's oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past.
Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal.
Houthis claim to have hit two military transport jets
The Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks.
On Tuesday afternoon, civil defense authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh.
The Houthis said they had repelled an advance by forces they described as Saudi-backed from the southern approaches to the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces earlier this month pushed the Houthis out of coastal areas they had seized in September, loosening the group's grip on a vital Red Sea oil route.
Houthi media claims Saudi struck Mocha
Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni city of Mocha. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to reduce regional tensions.
Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the three countries in a mutual defence pact, authorised Egypt's military on Monday to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked.

articles.title: Romania says Russian sabotage network set fire to Brașov defense plant, two Belarusians and a Ukrainian are suspects
articles.body:
Romania’s intelligence service, the Serviciul Român de Informații (SRI), said it had uncovered a sabotage network coordinated from Russia. According to a statement from the agency, the network was behind a Sept. 14 fire at the Carfil defense plant in the city of Brașov.
An investigation carried out jointly with other intelligence agencies found that several people from former Soviet states were involved in the arson.
“The information obtained so far indicates that the network’s missions were not limited to Romania. Coordinators in the Russian Federation had assigned it a wide range of targets in the region: state-owned and private weapons production facilities, as well as other targets of military and industrial interest.”
Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, or DIICOT, separately said that two Belarusian citizens and one Ukrainian citizen are suspected of involvement in the Brașov sabotage operation. Romanian authorities have issued arrest warrants for all three individuals. Two suspects were detained in Germany “while they were preparing to commit similar acts,” DIICOT said. Another suspect is in Poland.
In recent months, investigations have also uncovered other attempted acts of sabotage in Romania, including at international military facilities and sites used to train members of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the SRI said.
According to the intelligence service, operatives are typically recruited through social media. They are initially offered money to carry out a small task, such as watching or photographing a site, but the assignments then become progressively more serious. Over time, they can include assaults, arson, and even attempted killings. If a recruit refuses, the network’s handlers may resort to pressure and blackmail.
“These networks primarily exploit financial vulnerabilities, addictions, or criminal histories. To conceal their identities and movements, their members frequently use transportation, lodging, and payment methods registered under other people’s names, as well as communications via SIM cards from third countries and encrypted messaging apps.”
Authorities in Poland, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Germany, Lithuania, and Denmark have previously reported sabotage targeting defense companies and facilities involved in supporting Ukraine. Officials in those countries have accused Russian intelligence services of organizing the operations, while the people carrying them out have most often been Ukrainian citizens or nationals of EU member states.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi group claimed Tuesday that it targeted the Ras Tanura oil refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia with a ballistic missile, Anadolu reports.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on US social media company X that the group’s forces fired a ballistic missile at the refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province.
Saree claimed the missile hit its target and caused large fires at the site.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claim.
Earlier Tuesday, Saudi Civil Defense activated early warning alerts over a potential threat in Najran, Abha and Khamis Mushait before later announcing that the danger had passed, without specifying its nature.
READ: Saudi-led coalition intercepts 10 Houthi ballistic missiles targeting southern Saudi Arabia
The development comes amid continued military escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four drones and three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have intensified attacks against the kingdom since July, with missile and drone launches targeting civilian airports, oil facilities and military sites in the country increasing during October.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the Yemeni government against the Houthis since March 2015. The group, accused of receiving Iranian support, has controlled the capital Sanaa and other parts of Yemen since September 2014.
READ: Riyadh airport partially resumes flights after Houthi attacks

articles.title: Ukraine-Moldova Defense Deal Covers Air Defense, Cybersecurity and Joint R&D
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Ukraine-Moldova Defense Deal Covers Air Defense, Cybersecurity and Joint R&D
Ukraine and Moldova signed a five-year military-technical cooperation agreement covering defense technology, air defense, cyber defense, equipment maintenance, and joint research projects, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence reported on October 26.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Moldovan Defence Minister Anatolie Nosatîi signed the agreement in the presence of Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi and Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The agreement creates a framework for exchanging technologies, practical knowledge, and battlefield experience while developing joint defense projects.
“Ukraine has experience that cannot be gained through exercises,” Khmara stated. “We are ready to share this knowledge with our partners and help them better understand the equipment’s capabilities and use it more effectively.”
Khmara added that Ukraine is already advising Moldova on the development of its air defense capabilities.
“Our task is to strengthen our own defense and help our partners become more resilient to modern threats,” he stated.
The agreement covers the modernization, repair, and maintenance of military equipment, as well as cooperation on logistics, engineering, and protection of personnel and critical infrastructure.
The two countries will also work together on specialist training, testing and evaluation of military products, technology transfers, and the development and procurement of military equipment.
Other areas include joint research and development related to military production and capability development in cyber defense, surveillance, and airspace protection.
Cooperation will primarily take the form of consultations, exchanges of technical and scientific information, professional experience, and joint work on selected projects.
The agreement will remain in force for five years and can be extended automatically. Ukraine’s Defence Ministry stressed that its implementation will not affect Moldova’s constitutionally enshrined neutral status.
The agreement comes as Russia has repeatedly violated Moldova’s airspace during its war against Ukraine. UNITED24 Media reported that Moldovan airspace has been violated more than 100 times since the full-scale invasion began, prompting Chișinău to adopt Ukrainian anti-drone tactics.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Shoot-down rate of Russian jet-powered drones steadily increasing, General Staff says
articles.body:
Shoot-down rate of Russian jet-powered drones steadily increasing, General Staff says
According to an analysis of the last three months, Ukraine's average shoot-down rate for Russian Geran-4 UAVs is almost 60%, and the interception rate for jet-powered drones is steadily increasing.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Details: The military noted that during individual attacks, the shoot-down rate for jet-powered UAVs can reach 80%.
Quote: "Tactical aviation – F-16, Mirage and MiG-29 aircraft – currently plays a significant role in destroying jet-powered UAVs. At the same time, strengthening our short-range air defence (SHORAD) amid a shortage of surface-to-air guided missiles is a key issue that is currently receiving considerable attention."
Details: The General Staff explained that SHORAD includes anti-aircraft gun systems such as Gepard and Shilka, the latest Skynex, Skyranger and Terrahawk Paladin systems, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups from all components of the Ukrainian defence forces.
Quote: "Mobile fire groups are equipped not only with machine guns and associated equipment, but also with man-portable air defence systems (MANPADS). Using MANPADS, our warriors are now shooting down the enemy's jet-powered drones quite successfully."
Details: Meanwhile, work is constantly under way to reduce the cost of countering such air threats. In particular, testing of new interceptors is ongoing. According to the General Staff, some models have already shot down "several dozen Russian jet-powered Gerans".
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Russians had begun using a modification of the Geran-5 jet-powered UAV called Geran-5 K5-K.
- Two Ukrainian teams are also preparing domestically developed surface-to-air missiles for combat use against Russian jet-powered drones. In addition, Ukraine is already employing seven interceptors that have successfully shot down Russian jet-powered drones.
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia strikes Ukraine with 16 ballistic missiles – video
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia strikes Ukraine with 16 ballistic missiles – video
Russia attacked Ukraine with 16 ballistic missiles on the night of 26-27 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "In total, 16 ballistic missiles were launched overnight. More than 280 drones as well. Tragically, there have been casualties and hits in Kyiv, including on the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge. A serious escalation in Russia's operation against our logistics. There were also strikes on Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson and Chernivtsi oblasts. Almost everywhere, Russia's targets were the energy sector, logistics and ordinary urban infrastructure."
Details: Zelenskyy said that 12 people were injured following a Russian strike on a university campus and the surrounding area on the evening of 26 October, five of whom are students and university staff. Whilst emergency services were assisting people and dealing with the aftermath of the first strike, the Russians deployed ballistic missiles again.
The president emphasised: "The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which unfortunately have occurred recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the objectives of its terrorist campaign."
Background:
- On the night of 26-27 October, the Russians attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 280 Shahed (69 jet-powered) and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoy UAVs. The city of Kyiv was the main target of the attack.
- Early reports indicated that as of 09:00 of 27 October, Ukrainian air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 257 Russian aerial assets: two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 255 Shahed (56 jet-powered), Gerbera and other types of drones.
- On 26 October, Zelenskyy announced that Kyiv had been waiting for nearly a month for Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems, and instructed his team to discuss the matter with the US side again.
