articles.title: Caught stealing: An employee of Russia’s top-secret Department K has been convicted of selling a classified database
articles.body:
On Sept. 10, the Khimki City Court in suburban Moscow sentenced Anton Nesterov, a senior operative of the Bureau of Special Technical Measures (BSTM) of Russia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, to 13 years in a maximum-security penal colony. Nesterov was found guilty of selling a classified Federal Security Service (FSB) database to a hacker, taking a bribe, and gaining unlawful access to computer information. The defendant pleaded guilty only in part and refused to name his accomplices. However, The Insider has established Nesterov’s connections and learned additional details of his criminal case. The BSTM unit where Nesterov served is overseen by Department K of the FSB’s Economic Security Service and has a reputation as the most corrupt and scandal-ridden in the Russian law enforcement system.
The criminal case against Nesterov
According to the prosecution, Nesterov copied onto a flash drive a classified FSB database containing compromising material on the leadership of Russia’s Finance Ministry, the Central Bank, and several of the largest state banks, and then posted an advertisement for its sale on the internet. A hacker, whose name has not been disclosed, responded to the ad and offered 9 million rubles ($108,800) for the files.
From here, however, the accounts diverge. According to one version, FSB operatives supposedly detained the buyer before he could acquire the classified data. According to another, the hacker succeeded in buying the database, was subsequently detained, then struck a deal with investigators and testified against Nesterov.
Still though, according to The Insider’s source, the buyer was an informant from the hacker community cooperating with Department K of the FSB’s Economic Security Service (ESS), and in addition to the theft of the secret database, investigators looked into Nesterov’s involvement in extorting a large bribe from the management of the construction company PIK. After all, more than 20 different contacts labeled “PIK” were purportedly found in his phone.
The Insider previously reported on PIK owner Sergei Gordeev’s connections, and his real estate development company is at the heart of this story as well. In 2025, when the firm refused to pay a bribe, Nesterov allegedly organized a DDoS attack on the Lovit internet provider, which serves PIK’s new developments in Moscow and St. Petersburg. For unknown reasons though, this episode did not make it into the final version of the charges.
The criminal case was first heard at Moscow’s Basmanny Court. At the defense counsel’s request, the hearings were then moved to the Moscow Region city of Khimki, the defendant’s official place of residence (although Nesterov had lived for several years in the Edem gated community near Solnechnogorsk). Among those summoned for questioning was Nesterov’s older brother, Ilya, who works as an auditor at Sheremetyevo Airport. He told the investigator that he knew nothing about his brother’s double life.
The Khimki City Court, which sat behind closed doors, sentenced Nesterov to 13 years in a maximum-security penal colony. He will most likely serve his term in Penal Colony No. 11 in the city of Bor, Nizhny Novgorod Region, which holds former officers of the FSB, Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), Federal Protective Service (FSO), Interior Ministry, and Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) — a penitentiary facility The Insider also previously reported on.
Nesterov’s career
Anton Nesterov was born in 1992 in Ulyanovsk and developed an interest in computers early on. As a young man, he worked as an engineer at the Signal plant. In 2014, he took his father’s advice and enrolled in the Voronezh Institute of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, joining the department of radio engineering and electronics — a program known for training students from Belarus, Tajikistan, Azerbaijan, Mongolia, and Angola, alongside Russians.
After the institute, Nesterov was assigned to the ministry’s Bureau of Special Technical Measures (BSTM), where he rose to become a senior operative at the 4th section of the 40th department, handling financial crimes committed with the use of information technology and working under the supervision of the FSB’s Department K.
The 40th department, where Nesterov served, is considered the most corrupt and scandal-ridden unit within the BSTM. “They control all the well-known hackers. The guys from the 40th department drive decrepit Soviet vehicles to work, while in their garages they have posh cars registered to relatives and mistresses,” a Ministry of Internal Affairs source told The Insider.
During interrogations, Nesterov refused to name accomplices and took all the blame. However, The Insider’s source is confident that the operative most likely had accomplices from the FSB or the BSTM: “He sat in the FSB compound on Bolshaya Lubyanka Street and worked in tandem with guys from the FSB. It is hard to believe that Anton pulled it all off alone.”
“He sat in the FSB compound on Bolshaya Lubyanka Street and worked in tandem with guys from the FSB. It is hard to believe that Anton pulled it all off alone”
Fugitives from the BSTM and mysterious deaths in Mexico
The Bureau of Special Technical Measures was established in 1992 to combat the illegal distribution of radio-electronic and special technical equipment, electronic payment fraud, terrorism, incitement of ethnic hatred, and child pornography online. It excels in various technological tricks for surveillance and data interception and has at its disposal several direction-finding vehicles with extendable antennas capable of eavesdropping on any cell phone from a distance of 20 km. As a rule, these minibuses and GAZelles are disguised as vehicles marked “Refrigerator repair” or “We install windows.” Some of these special vehicles have been transferred to the occupied territories of Ukraine to track phone calls.
How effective these devices are in practice, however, is unclear. Raisa Parshina, owner of the Far Eastern Transport Group, told The Insider that when her son Maxim was kidnapped in 2005 and a ransom of $7 million was demanded, acquaintances advised her to turn privately to the BSTM to triangulate the incoming numbers. She met with employees of the bureau and was told that a direction finder costs $10,000 a day. Parshina agreed, but a week later she was told that no results had been obtained.
Regional BSTM units operate in all the main directorates of Russia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, also carrying out tasks for their colleagues at the FSB. Since the Bureau’s creation, nearly all key positions have been held by former FSB officers.
Since 2017, BSTM has been headed by Lieutenant General Mikhail Litvinov, who previously worked as deputy head of the FSB’s 12th Center — responsible for tapping phones, monitoring internet traffic, and intercepting information from technical communication channels. Litvinov’s office was located in downtown Moscow, at 26 Myasnitskaya Street, next door to three units of the FSB’s Operational Search Directorate (military units 52295, 96586, and 98933). For secrecy he was listed as head of the Center for Applied Research and supposedly engaged in studying public opinion.
Incidentally, since 2019 bailiffs from Moscow’s Zyuzino district have been unable to “squeeze” 46,668 rubles ($578) in taxes out of the general, left unpaid from his time working at the Center.
The appointment of Litvinov allowed the FSB to take the BSTM under its control, and the bureau expanded its remit to cover the wiretapping and surveillance of anti-Kremlin opposition figures and independent journalists.
However, in 2023 Litvinov was on the verge of dismissal after his subordinates — Georgy Satyukov, head of the 3rd section of the BSTM’s 40th department, and Dmitry Sokolov, a former colleague from Tyumen — fled abroad. According to the investigation, Sokolov’s brokering helped Satyukov secure a bribe of almost 5 billion rubles ($62 million) in bitcoin from Alexei Ivanov (Bilyuchenko), co-founder of the crypto exchange BTC, who was seeking the closure of a criminal case.
Satyukov received almost $62 million in bitcoin as a bribe for the closure of the criminal case against BTC founder Alexei Ivanov
The correspondence and phone conversations of Satyukov, Sokolov, and the crypto tycoon Ivanov were recorded by the FSB’s 12th Center, where General Litvinov used to serve. Shortly before their arrest, the corrupt operatives were tipped off by accomplices from the FSB and the BSTM, allowing them to flee the country.
It remained unclear how the fugitives crossed the border, since their passports were supposed to be kept in General Litvinov’s safe, and during questioning, the general denied having handed over the documents.
Following a suit by Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office, the state seized millions of dollars’ worth of real estate from Satyukov: 13 apartments in Moscow and St. Petersburg (including a 200-square-meter unit in the elite Moscow complex Nezhinsky Kovcheg), and 11 non-residential properties in Saratov, Izhevsk, and the Sverdlovsk Region. His mansion in the UAE is currently frozen.
From Sokolov, the authorities confiscated: a nearly 500-square-meter apartment in St. Petersburg valued at 400 million rubles ($4.96 million), three luxury apartments on Kamenny Island, and a mansion in a historic district of the Petrograd Side. At the request of the Prosecutor General’s Office, the authorities in Dubai also froze Sokolov’s apartment in the Burj Khalifa tower.
Then, in 2024, Satyukov and Sokolov supposedly died in Mexico — one after the other, even if investigators suspect their deaths have been faked. In a conversation with The Insider, investigative journalist Andrei Zakharov said that phone billing records of the “dead” Satyukov and Sokolov feature the same BSTM operatives whom Nesterov called, along with three dozen alleged crypto figures, hackers, and businessmen from all over Russia.
Still, a source at the FSB told The Insider that after Nesterov’s imprisonment, BSTM head Litvinov is unlikely to keep his seat. Most likely, he will be given an order and sent off to a well-earned retirement.

articles.title: Guns fall silent around Russian-occupied Oleshky so its starving residents can get aid, but Russia’s guarantees remain secret
articles.body:
A ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast took effect at 03:00 on 27 October Kyiv time, and both sides were complying with the agreements, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said. Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that its forces had stopped firing on the Kherson axis at 04:00 Moscow time, at the same moment.
Russia has kept Oleshky cut off for months. In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine documented worsening shortages of food, medicine, and medical care there and in neighboring Hola Prystan. As of 8 October, Lubinets’ office still saw no practical breakthrough toward an organized evacuation, with 358 residents verified as needing help to leave. The ceasefire is the first step that has to hold before aid can go in and residents can leave, an operation Marc Beckman, the first lady’s chief adviser, expects to take five to seven days.
By 09:00 on 27 October, Russian forces were still observing the ceasefire, according to Pavlo Drohal, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 30th Marine Corps. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Presidential Office, announced that the mission had begun and that Lubinets had gone to the site to coordinate it.
Ceasefire brought forward by two days
The White House announced on 23 October that First Lady Melania Trump had secured a localized ceasefire, set to begin on 29 October. The same evening, Russia’s chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced a ceasefire on the Kherson axis from 27 October, with engineering reconnaissance and a secured route for a humanitarian convoy. Ukraine’s General Staff followed, introducing a ceasefire in a designated area from the same hour.
Beckman told Ukrinform on 26 October that Russia had moved the ceasefire two days earlier and extended it beyond Oleshky into Kherson Oblast. Lubinets said on 23 October that the mission should effectively begin on 29 October, after demining, adding that the date was not a matter of principle for either side.
A day after the announcement, Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, who lead the two negotiating groups, confirmed the timing in an online meeting, he said. According to Lubinets, the agreement covers demining the road to Oleshky, delivering food, water, medicine, and hospital equipment, and safe movement for civilians.
Newsmax to document the operation
Meanwhile, Melania Trump said she had secured an “impartial American media organization” to accompany the Russian and Ukrainian teams. Beckman named it as Newsmax. He said he had worked directly with the channel’s owner, and that its journalists would record testimony as what he called neutral American observers.
Residents could leave for Ukraine or Russia, or stay, Beckman said. He added that Russia had assured Kyiv and Washington it would respect their choice of destination. Both governments asked him not to disclose what guarantees Russia gave or how violations would be handled, he said. He expects the operation to take five to seven days after 29 October, with an extension possible if both sides agree.
Diplomat doubts the truce will move peace talks
At the same time, Kostiantyn Yelisieiev, Ukraine’s ambassador to the EU in 2010–2015, told Radio NV the truce became possible only through the personal involvement of Donald and Melania Trump. The US president, he said, sees it as a way to show Americans he is bringing peace closer. He said he expects Russia to attempt provocations aimed at pushing residents toward the Russian side.
Yelisieiev said he does not share the optimism of those who think Oleshky could push the wider peace process forward. He compared it to the Black Sea grain corridor, a one-off arrangement that no longer works. He warned of a “diplomatic smokescreen”: Russia imitates negotiations while it keeps fighting, hoping Ukraine and its partners weaken over time.
A town under blockade
Oleshky lies on the left bank of the Dnipro, about 4 km from Kherson, and has been occupied since February 2022, Radio Svoboda reported. The White House says it had about 24,000 residents before the war and estimates 1,700 to 2,000 remain, mostly elderly, including about 50 children. Russian troops have also seized food dropped by Ukrainian drones, a local official said.

- Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say

articles.title: Russia strikes military-industrial enterprises, transport infrastructure in Kiev overnight
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian forces launched a large-scale overnight attack, hitting military-industrial enterprises and transport infrastructure facilities in Kiev, a logistics center in Kharkov Region, as well as maritime vessels supporting Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has summarized the main information about the targets struck.
Defense Ministry report
Russian forces conducted a massive overnight strike against targets in Ukraine using precision-guided ground-based weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
According to the ministry, the strike targeted Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises engaged in the production and storage of cruise missiles and long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, transport infrastructure facilities in Kiev, a logistics center in Kharkov Region, as well as maritime vessels used to support the Ukrainian army.
Targets hit
The Russian Defense Ministry later clarified that Russian forces had struck an industrial enterprise in Kiev engaged in the production and storage of long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles.
A workshop in Kiev operated by OAKLINE LLC was also hit. The facility is used to assemble and store Fire Point’s long-and medium-range FP-1 and FP-2 unmanned aerial vehicles.
In addition, Russian forces struck the Yuzhny road-and-rail bridge in Kiev, which serves to carry military cargo by road and rail.
A loading and customs terminal run by Regional Logistics Center was also hit in Kharkov Region. The facility is used to store and distribute materiel and dual-use cargo destined to support the Ukrainian army, as well as reconnaissance and strike drones.
In addition, a cargo ship carrying supplies to support the Ukrainian army was struck at sea while heading to the port of Chernomorsk in Odessa Region.
Situation in Ukraine
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said on his Telegram channel that the Yuzhny Bridge across the Dnieper River had sustained damage. Explosions were reported in the capital overnight, and an air raid alert was issued.
He also reported damage to metro infrastructure, noting that one of the subway lines crosses the bridge.
According to the city administration’s Telegram channel, traffic across the Yuzhny Bridge has been restricted, and metro trains are temporarily suspended.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact Courts Iran: Containment Comes Full Circle
articles.body:
For nearly half a century, Iran’s adversaries have tried to isolate it, intimidate it, sanction it into submission and bomb it into irrelevance. Now, in a remarkable inversion of regional power politics, three countries historically invested in its containment have arrived in Tehran to discuss their security with the very state they were supposed to marginalise.
The country they could not defeat is becoming the country they cannot afford to ignore.
Yesterday, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın met Iranian officials in an encounter whose diplomatic courtesies barely concealed its strategic significance.
The Mecca Pact, the joint defence agreement that Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed in Mecca in August, was supposed to consolidate a formidable Sunni-led defence alignment. Yet its representatives have come to Tehran confronting an inconvenient reality: Iran cannot be excluded from regional security merely because Washington and its partners find its independence intolerable.
Apparently, the Islamic Republic has become considerably more respectable since demonstrating that it cannot be conveniently eliminated.
This is the distinction between military destruction and strategic defeat that Washington and Israel persistently confuse. Overwhelming firepower can devastate infrastructure, assassinate officials and inflict enormous suffering. It cannot manufacture political submission.
Iran has survived military confrontation, retained retaliatory capabilities and forced neighbouring governments to reconsider the potentially catastrophic consequences of another war.
Survival becomes strategic victory when your adversaries must reorganise their calculations around it.
For Saudi Arabia, the reckoning is particularly humiliating. Riyadh spent decades treating American military supremacy as an insurance policy against Iranian influence. Yemen exposed the bankruptcy of that assumption.
Ansar Allah, Yemen’s Houthi movement, demonstrated that superior arsenals cannot guarantee security against an adversary capable of imposing disproportionate costs. The Saudi monarchy possesses spectacular weaponry, immense wealth and powerful patrons. Yet none of these has eliminated its vulnerability to Yemeni retaliation.
Now Riyadh finds itself seeking Tehran’s cooperation to manage a conflict that its military superiority has failed to resolve.
Evidently, purchasing American weapons is considerably easier than purchasing strategic security.
Pakistan’s predicament is scarcely less revealing. Munir presides over a military establishment accustomed to presenting strategic dependency as diplomatic sophistication. Islamabad’s defence commitments to Riyadh now threaten to entangle Pakistan in confrontations with Iran and Yemen that serve neither its geography nor its national interests.
The Mecca Pact promises collective security. Its less advertised feature is collective exposure to somebody else’s strategic miscalculations.
Munir must now reconcile his obligations to Saudi patrons with the inconvenient realities of Iranian power. It is an awkward assignment for an establishment that has repeatedly mistaken proximity to foreign power for genuine strategic independence.
Türkiye confronts a different calculation but reaches a similar conclusion. Ankara understands that NATO membership, military capabilities and regional ambitions cannot abolish geography. No credible security architecture can be constructed by pretending Iran is dispensable.
The deeper contradiction, however, lies within the Mecca Pact itself.
Its members seek the reassurance of collective defence while attempting to avoid being dragged into another American-Israeli confrontation. An attack on one may formally constitute an attack on all. But such commitments become considerably less attractive when Iranian retaliation, Yemeni escalation and vulnerable Gulf infrastructure enter the equation.
Collective defence sounds magnificent until someone presents the collective bill.
Iran’s achievement is not that its neighbours have embraced its revolutionary worldview. They have not. Saudi Arabia remains deeply connected to Washington, Pakistan continues its elaborate balancing act, and Türkiye remains embedded in NATO.
The significance runs deeper: these governments increasingly recognise that excluding Iran from regional security may expose them to greater dangers than engaging it.
That realisation strikes at the foundations of the American security paradigm.
For decades, Washington cultivated regional dependence on American protection while organising strategic anxieties around Iranian power. Now those same governments are exploring cooperation with the country they were encouraged to regard as an existential threat.
The irony is devastating. Decades of attempting to contain Iran may have helped establish its indispensability.
And Tehran, displaying the composure of a state conscious of its diplomatic leverage, has welcomed its visitors graciously. No triumphalist declarations are necessary. The spectacle speaks adequately for itself.
The Mecca Pact arrived ostensibly to discuss regional stability. What it encountered was the strategic consequence of its own failed assumptions.
Iran did not have to join the alliance. The alliance had to come to Iran.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Poland to host European Patriot maintenance centre, government says
articles.body:
WARSAW, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A maintenance centre for Lockheed Martin’s Patriot interceptor missiles will be established in Poland, Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on Tuesday.
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have strained stocks of air-defence interceptor missiles and caused delivery delays, prompting countries to seek maintenance and production capabilities closer to home.
“Four countries competed for the European location of this investment: alongside Poland — Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote on social media platform X. “This success was not a given,” she said.
The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the United States, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.
The Pentagon said, in a statement on its website, that the European Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Maintenance Facility (MMF) “will be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden.”
“By establishing regional maintenance, repair, and overhaul capabilities directly within the European theater, the MMF will dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines,” the statement said.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told reporters during a briefing in Brussels that the value of the investment would be around 1 billion zlotys ($253 million) and that it would take a dozen or so months to make the centre operational.
($1 = 3.9462 zlotys)
(Reporting by Karol Badohal, Anna Wlodarczak-Semczuk, Pawel Florkiewicz; Editing by Aidan Lewis and Tomasz Janowski)

articles.title: Russian court jails IT company director for 13 years over crypto donations after Binance shared his data, rights group says
articles.body:
A Russian court sentenced Yuri Belenky, director of the IT company DiHouse, to 13 years in prison on terrorism financing charges, Radio Liberty reported on 26 October. The case concerns cryptocurrency donations that investigators believe were meant for Ukraine’s Armed Forces, the outlet said. The court also fined Belenky 500,000 rubles ($6,200), according to the report.
Since 2022, Russian courts have imprisoned Russians and Ukrainians under treason, terrorism, and other national-security laws over donations to Ukrainian causes. Binance, one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, left Russia in 2023 but says it cooperates with lawful law-enforcement requests in different countries.
Belenky had lived in Bulgaria with his wife and child since 2015. In September 2025, he traveled to Moscow on business, and police detained him at the airport for allegedly using obscene language, Radio Liberty reported. In court, Belenky denied swearing, but the judge gave him 13 days of administrative detention. On the 10th day of his detention, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a criminal case against him under an article on terrorism financing, based on a report from the Federal Security Service, according to the report.
Binance shared account records with Russian investigators, rights group says
In October 2025, Russia’s Investigative Committee contacted Binance to request information on six users who had transferred funds to a cryptocurrency wallet published by journalist Arkady Babchenko, the Russian human rights project First Department said on 17 August 2026. The exchange provided investigators with Belenky’s detailed account history, including his personal information, copies of identification documents, and cryptocurrency transaction records, according to the organization. The human rights project said the materials helped investigators identify nine more transfers, which went into the final charge against Belenky. Binance told his lawyer it does not give law enforcement user account data without a court order or an equivalent ruling, the group said.
Belenky’s alleged offense was transferring donations totaling 126,000 rubles ($1,560) between 2022 and 2024 to an account published by Babchenko, Radio Liberty reported. The court ordered that sum confiscated.
Russia sentences Ukrainian women from Zaporizhzhia Oblast to 14 years for donating $120 to Ukrainian forces
The court said the money in Babchenko’s account went to Ukraine’s Armed Forces and the Azov battalion, which Russia designates as a terrorist organization, Radio Liberty reported.
In a statement dated 14 October 2025, Babchenko said he had not received transfers from Belenky to the cryptocurrency wallets he had published. He emphasized that he had raised money for civilian humanitarian needs, not to support the military.
Binance’s exit from Russia and previous data-sharing concerns
In September 2023, Binance announced that it would sell its entire Russian business to cryptocurrency exchange CommEX, according to the company’s website. Operating in Russia was incompatible with Binance’s compliance strategy, the exchange’s chief compliance officer, Noah Perlman, said in the announcement. Binance said it would fully exit the Russian market, receive no share of future revenue from the sale, and retain no option to buy back the business.
CommEX said on 29 September 2023 that it was not owned by Binance but confirmed that it had hired some former Binance employees during the platform’s six-month development, Cointelegraph reported.
UK sanctions crypto exchanges and “A7 network” in crackdown on Russian evasion systems
The exit came after earlier questions about Binance’s dealings with the Russian state. In April 2021, Russian financial intelligence officials met with Binance’s head of Eastern Europe and Russia in Moscow and asked the exchange to provide customer data, including names and addresses, Reuters reported in April 2022. The Binance executive agreed to the request in a message to a business associate, saying he didn’t have “much of a choice,” the outlet said. Binance told Reuters it had never been contacted by Russian authorities about Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny.
In February 2026, 11 US senators asked the Treasury Department and the Justice Department to investigate Binance’s compliance with sanctions and anti-money laundering rules, Cointelegraph reported. They cited reports that about $1.7 billion had moved through Binance to Iran-linked entities, as well as possible activity related to evading Russian sanctions. The senators also warned that Binance payment cards launched in parts of the former Soviet Union could facilitate sanctions evasion. Binance rejected the allegations.

articles.title: Russia attacks Kyiv university buildings, injuring five – video
articles.body:
Russia attacks Kyiv university buildings, injuring five – video
Five students and employees of the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE) were injured in a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on the night of 26-27 October. Early reports about people killed were not confirmed and there were no fatalities among students or employees.
Source: Andrii Butenko, Minister of Education and Science
Details: University buildings and student accommodation were also damaged SUTE is currently assessing the damage incurred. The Ministry of Education and Science reported that they are in contact with the institution's management to provide the necessary assistance.
SUTE reported that academic buildings and the campus territory sustained damage as a result of the overnight attack.
Anatolii Mazaraki, SUTE Vice-Chancellor, said that some people were in the shelter, while those injured were people who were outdoors, as reported by Ukrainian media outlet hromadske.
Thus, two sophomore students were injured near the student accommodation as a result of the Russian attack. They sustained severe injuries. One of them is currently awaiting surgery.
The SUTE Student Council calls for joining a fundraiser for the treatment of the students injured – Roman Balla and Anna Voloshyna.
Kyiv24 TV channel reports that currently, students and teachers are helping to deal with the aftermath of the attack.
Quote from Butenko: "This is yet another time the terrorist country has attacked educational institutions. Whether a university, a scientific institution, a college, a school or a kindergarten – the enemy directs its missiles against children, teachers, and scientists without any pity or humanity. There is no justification for Moscow's cynical actions."
Details: The minister also urged participants in the educational process to proceed immediately to shelters during an air-raid warning.
The Ministry of Youth and Sports reported that the Ivan Piddubny Olympic College was also damaged in the Russian attack. During the attack, the children were in a shelter and were therefore not injured.
Background:
- On the evening of 26 October and on the night of 26-27 October, the Russians struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the Russians launched 16 ballistic missiles over the night.
- The State Emergency Service of Ukraine noted that one person was killed and another 15 were injured.

articles.title: Satellite images confirm damage at Russia’s largest known air defense storage base after Ukrainian drone strike
articles.body:
Satellite images show signs of fires at the 75th Arsenal facility in Serpukhov in the Moscow Region, around 60 miles south of the Russian capital, Greenpeace analysts who examined the imagery told The Insider. The site was struck by Ukrainian drones overnight into Oct. 22. The target was the largest known Russian storage base for air defense equipment.
Satellite images from Oct. 26 show changes compared with earlier imagery. Greenpeace experts who analyzed the data told The Insider that burn marks are visible in the upper left of the image. Additional signs of fire can be seen in the center near a hangar and in the lower left.
The Ukrainian open source intelligence (OSINT) project Oko Hora ✙ News and Analytics claims that the strikes hit workshops No. 24 and No. 25, which specialize in repairing and restoring components for Russia’s S-300V and Buk surface-to-air missile systems, its Tunguska-M air defense systems, and radar equipment. The site, formerly an arsenal of the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate (GRAU), only became the largest known storage base for air defense equipment in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
OSINT analyst Jompy wrote in March 2024 that researchers had identified an air defense equipment storage base at the 75th Arsenal site in Serpukhov, adding that the facility had originally served as an artillery depot before being repurposed to store air defense systems. Satellite images show numerous hangars at the site that may contain systems including the Buk or S-300. The analyst said it appeared to be the largest known storage base for air defense and surface-to-air missile systems in Russia.
Another OSINT analyst, Athene Noctua, wrote in June 2024 that the 75th Arsenal base held about 60% of the identified reserve of Russian Ground Forces air defense equipment — 574 out of 950 units.

articles.title: Turkey committee approves pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkish parliamentary committee approves defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
A Turkish parliamentary committee approved a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Tuesday, as tensions between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels grow.
The defence agreement commits the sides to regard an armed attack against one as an attack on all three. The foreign affairs committee approved it with votes from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party and its allies, despite objections from the opposition.
The agreement now goes to the full assembly for a debate and a vote. No date has been set.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defence Agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, joint weapons production, technology transfers and intelligence sharing. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, according to the agreement published by Turkish state media.
Ministers from the grouping have already met twice, in Istanbul and Riyadh, while high-level delegations from the three countries held talks in Tehran on Monday to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Turkish government officials say they are considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, but that the agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Ruling Justice and Development Party legislator Fuat Oktay, who heads the committee, urged fellow members to approve the pact, arguing that it aims to increase deterrence and cooperation, does not target other countries and is likely to contribute to peace and stability.
"The agreements our country has signed and to which it is a party are not intended for aggression, expansionism, or the formation of a bloc against third countries," Oktay said.
"On the contrary, our nation is a party to defence agreements aimed at strengthening deterrence, fortifying our region and fostering peace and stability."
Opposition parties warned the agreement could put Turkish soldiers in harm's way and embroil the country in other nations' conflicts.
"Will this agreement enhance the security of the peoples involved, or will it create new obligations that entangle Turkey in the wars of other nations?" asked Semra Caglar Gokalp of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party.
Pointing to conflicts between Pakistan and India and tensions along Pakistan's border with Afghanistan, she continued: "What are the limits of the responsibility Turkey might assume in the face of these challenges?"
The opposition has also criticised the parties for holding meetings before parliament has ratified the pact.

articles.title: European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
articles.body:
European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has branded European leaders “political masochists,” accusing them of sacrificing their own citizens’ welfare in pursuit of Russia’s defeat in Ukraine.
Speaking to editors-in-chief of African media outlets in Moscow on Tuesday, Lavrov accused Western governments of pressuring their populations to accept declining living standards to secure Ukraine’s victory in conflict with Russia. 
“They are trying to keep public opinion in a position where people must sacrifice everything: salaries, jobs, healthcare services and social benefits in general, so that Ukraine defeats Russia,” Lavrov said. “People can feel how their situation is deteriorating in European countries,” he added.
He singled out German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as one of the politicians advocating such an approach. “These are masochists, political masochists, if you like,” the foreign minister said.
Merz has defended Germany’s growing military spending and continued support for Kiev while warning that the country can no longer afford its existing welfare system.
The German government has tightened welfare rules, introducing benefit reductions of 30% for repeated violations and, in some cases, complete withdrawal. Berlin’s proposed 2027 budget also envisages billions of euros in savings from pensions, healthcare and other social programs.
Germany has meanwhile earmarked €11.6 billion for Ukraine in 2027, alongside plans to raise defense spending to record levels.
Britain, another major backer of Kiev, has also reduced welfare payments, nearly halving health-related benefits for most new claimants under Universal Credit, a program supporting low-income households and people unable to work.
In September, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called for further welfare cuts to fund increased military spending. “We need to fund our defence, not spend all our money on welfare,” she said. The government, however, rejected her proposal.
France has likewise pursued spending restraint, including a proposed public-sector pay freeze, while increasing military expenditure. The measures have faced opposition from trade unions protesting declining purchasing power and deteriorating public services.
Public discontent has fueled widespread protests across Europe in recent weeks, with hundreds of thousands demonstrating in France over rising living costs, education funding and inequality. Tens of thousands have also taken to the streets in Spain and Portugal over soaring housing costs, while Italy has seen protests over declining living standards.
European NATO members have committed to substantially increasing defense expenditure, citing the perceived threat from Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin last week rejected repeated claims that Moscow was preparing for war with Europe, describing them as part of an ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. “They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass,” Putin stated.
Moscow has repeatedly dismissed claims that it intends to attack NATO countries as “nonsense,” accusing Western leaders of using the alleged Russian threat to justify militarization and continued support for Kiev.

articles.title: Iran and “Mecca Pact” countries agree to continue talks amid fears of renewed regional conflict
articles.body:
Iran and representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to continue diplomatic discussions following an initial meeting in Tehran, amid growing concerns over a renewed escalation of conflict in the Middle East.
The talks brought together officials from the three countries that signed the “Mecca Pact” joint defence agreement, as regional tensions intensify following renewed hostilities involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman traveled to Tehran for the meeting, alongside Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and other senior officials.
According to a statement from the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the delegation’s visit was intended to “de-escalate the current crisis and promote dialogue and diplomatic solutions.”
Iranian state television reported Monday that the participants had agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation, including in the areas of regional peace and security.
The meeting took place amid warnings from the United States and Israel concerning the possibility of renewed military hostilities in the region.
It marked the first joint visit to Tehran by senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey since the three countries established their defence alliance last August.
READ: Mecca Defense Alliance agrees to ‘immediately’ implement collective defense commitments
The diplomatic initiative comes against the backdrop of renewed confrontations between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthi movement, which resumed in July following the collapse of a truce that had been in place in Yemen since 2022.
Riyadh supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government, while the Houthis remain a major force in the country’s prolonged conflict.
The talks also coincided with the Egyptian parliament’s approval of defence support for Saudi Arabia in response to Houthi attacks originating from Yemen.
Regional tensions have intensified ahead of Israel’s parliamentary elections scheduled for Tuesday, 27th October, and the US midterm elections the following week, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is seeking to retain control of both chambers of Congress.
As the discussions began in Tehran on Monday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for urgent efforts to prevent further regional escalation.
“It is urgent to put an end to any escalation,” Guterres said, emphasizing the need to contain tensions as diplomatic efforts continue.
The agreement to maintain discussions signals a continued diplomatic effort by Iran and the three countries to address regional security concerns, although no specific commitments or outcomes beyond further talks were announced.
READ: Iran, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia agree to continue regional security cooperation

articles.title: Air Force Spokesperson: Russian forces launch several ballistic missile strikes on Pivdenny Bridge in Kyiv
articles.body:
During the latest attack, Russian forces launched several ballistic missile strikes against the Southern Bridge (Pivdenny) in Kyiv. While such structures are not easily destroyed, repairing the damaged bridge deck will take time, Yuriy Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, stated during a televised marathon on Tuesday.
"Of course, the bridge deck can be repaired—bridges are not as easy to destroy as some might think. Nevertheless, this does cause certain inconveniences, and repairs will take time," Ihnat said.
According to him, the adversary employed 16 ballistic missiles—either Iskander-M missiles or S-400 surface-to-air guided missiles—during the recent attack. Specialists examining the impact site will determine the exact type of missiles used. "The adversary used two types of missiles today: either Iskander-M or S-400 surface-to-air missiles," the spokesperson noted.
Ihnat emphasized that over the past two weeks, Russian forces have focused their missile strikes on Kyiv, launching ballistic missiles in several waves throughout the night and combining them with drone attacks.
"Previously, ballistic missile strikes might have occurred just once a night. Now, they are spread out over several waves of attacks... They launch these strikes in waves, and all of this is accompanied by drone attacks," he said.
As previously reported, Taras Chmut, head of the Come Back Alive foundation and a military analyst, stated in an interview with DW that the complete destruction of bridges in Kyiv by Russian shelling is a possibility, provided the adversary is willing to commit significant resources. At the same time, he noted that destroying a single section of a bridge does not necessarily lead to the collapse of the entire structure; the critical issue remains how quickly a crossing can be restored, at least in some capacity. According to him, even partial damage to bridges could severely complicate urban logistics, particularly the operation of the metro system and public transport.
"I wouldn't rule out such a scenario; if the Russians are determined enough and willing to expend the necessary resources, they could certainly do it," he emphasized.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that on Tuesday, the enemy struck the Pivdenny Bridge in Kyiv, damaging metro infrastructure located on the span.
Kyiv Metro has temporarily suspended service between Osokorky and Chervony Khutir stations on the green line due to the damage to infrastructure on the Pivdenny Bridge. Furthermore, with the Pivdenny Bridge closed, both freight and passenger vehicle traffic have been diverted along alternative routes.

articles.title: Zelensky: Europe Must Be Included in November Peace Talks
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky insisted Tuesday, Oct. 27, that European countries must be involved in upcoming peace negotiations, warning that no European partner should be excluded from decisions on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
His remarks came as preparations continued for US-mediated talks involving Ukrainian, American and Russian representatives in November, following renewed diplomatic contacts between Moscow and European leaders.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We expect a trilateral format in November, with Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives,” Zelensky said in his evening address.
“It is important that Europe also take part in all diplomatic moves. Ukraine has always insisted that Europe must be present and must have a say in the decisions,” he said.
“And this, by the way, applies to everyone in Europe. No one should be left out of the process.”
The Ukrainian president’s comments underscored Kyiv’s position that any settlement must address not only Ukraine’s future but also the security interests of European countries affected by Russia’s war.
The anticipated negotiations are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, according to statements from Moscow. Discussions are being prepared at the level of negotiating teams, rather than as a summit of the three countries’ presidents.
Nordic leaders hold rare direct talks with Putin
Zelensky’s appeal followed a rare phone call on Tuesday between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Trump Administration Weighs Lifting Sanctions on Kremlin’s Investment Fund – NYT
The call, conducted from Helsinki, was initiated by Finland and Norway in consultation with Ukraine and followed diplomatic discussions held in Oslo on Oct. 20.
According to a joint statement published by the Norwegian government, the Nordic leaders sought to convey messages directly to Putin about future negotiations and the need to end the war.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said, emphasizing that the outcome of the war would directly affect European security.
“Ending the war requires direct discussions,” he added.
Støre stressed the war’s human and economic consequences and said the leaders had called for de-escalation.
Both leaders reaffirmed their continued support for Ukraine.
Zelensky briefed after Putin call
Following the conversation with Putin, Stubb and Støre briefed Zelensky on the discussions.
According to the Ukrainian president’s office, the Nordic leaders told Putin that Russia needed to take concrete steps toward de-escalation, particularly by reducing attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelensky thanked them for coordinating the initiative with Kyiv and supporting efforts to bring Moscow back to negotiations.
The leaders also discussed preparations for the November trilateral meeting and possible formats for broader European participation.
Finland and Norway, both of which share borders with Russia, have a particular interest in reliable security arrangements, Zelensky noted.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, said the participants had welcomed plans to resume trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.
Moscow reiterated its position that any lasting settlement must take account of what it describes as Russia’s security interests.
Kyiv seeks united European approach ahead of negotiations
In his evening address, Zelensky said Ukraine was intensifying diplomatic coordination with European partners while working to secure additional military assistance ahead of the anticipated negotiations.
“These days, we are doing our best to secure new support packages,” he said.
“Coordination with our partners is also ongoing to ensure diplomacy and meetings as soon as possible.”
Zelensky also confirmed that Kyiv would remain in contact with Washington as preparations continued.
The renewed diplomatic push follows talks in Oslo involving Zelensky, European leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who subsequently met Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
Following those contacts, both Kyiv and Moscow expressed support for resuming trilateral negotiations, which had stalled after earlier rounds produced limited progress beyond prisoner exchanges.

articles.title: Iran, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia agree to continue regional security cooperation

Iran, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have agreed to continue dialogue to strengthen cooperation on regional peace and security, according to a joint statement issued after a four-way meeting in Tehran.
The statement said the four countries had agreed to continue dialogue to enhance cooperation, including in the fields of regional peace and security.

Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin also attended.

Participants agreed to continue talks to strengthen cooperation among the four countries.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry also said Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi attended a meeting between President Masoud Pezeshkian and representatives responsible for defence and security affairs from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: An EU country has reopened the Russia channel. What brought it back?
articles.body:
An EU country has reopened the Russia channel. What brought it back?
On October 26, 2026, the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission resumed its work. The announcement was made during Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s visit to Moscow for WWII Victory Day celebrations. The timing of the meeting is particularly favorable for the ruling coalition led by Fico’s SMER party. The only event that somewhat dampened the occasion was the defeat of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic’s party in snap elections in Serbia. Vucic’s foreign policy has often been likened to Fico’s approach in Slovakia. Below, we explore why these stories are fundamentally different and what is really happening in the context of Russia-Slovakia relations, as well as in Slovakia itself, ahead of the election on September 26, 2027.
Perfect timing
Although the resumption of the intergovernmental commission was announced in May, the talks did not take place until six months later. On the Slovak side, they were led by a close ally of Fico and the current foreign affairs minister, Juraj Blanar. The lists of negotiators on both sides were not disclosed until the last moment. The date of the negotiations was also shrouded in secrecy and was not revealed until last week during an EU summit, which, according to reports, was marked by a “terrible” atmosphere and was “unworthy of a meeting of the European Council.”
Fico’s attendance was uncertain right up to the last minute, with Bratislava skillfully playing this card. Slovak diplomats maintained suspense, suggesting that Fico’s visit depended on the “substantiality of concessions,” keeping the EU on its toes regarding a possible geopolitical demarche. Ultimately, Fico stayed in Bratislava, crafting a perfect political alibi before Brussels while sending a full government delegation to Moscow to tackle pressing political and economic challenges. He skillfully employed this maneuver, illustrating that in today’s landscape, ‘glitch-art diplomacy’ – characterized by protocol breaches, unpredictability, and exploiting systemic errors – remains effective. Though not large in size, Slovakia is a critical node through which the East and West continue to exchange signals.
The timing of this event strikes a perfect balance for the ruling authorities, both in terms of domestic political dynamics and the wider European context. First, municipal elections held in Slovakia over the past weekend confirmed the strength of the current coalition. Fico and his allies demonstrated their dominance across regions and industrial hubs, leaving the pro-Western opposition confined to Bratislava. This electoral victory has secured a solid backing for the prime minister, giving him the freedom to pursue bold foreign policy initiatives.
The external context vividly illustrated to the Slovak audience the validity of the ruling coalition’s stance. The recent EU summit only deepened the rift among allies. The European Commission attempted to impose new climate quotas, but the countries of the Visegrad Group clearly expressed their dissent, with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis openly criticizing Ursula von der Leyen for her ‘green transition’ dogmas. This unfolded against the backdrop of a shocking report from Eurostat, revealing that most EU countries are facing budget deficits, with the highest figures recorded in Hungary (7.2%) and Romania (9.2%).
Amid this dismal European landscape, news from Slovakia underscores the looming threat of deindustrialization. German automotive giant Porsche recently announced its decision to shift production of its Cayenne model from Bratislava back to Leipzig, aiming to salvage its parent company’s facilities in Germany, which are struggling due to the energy crisis. The risk of German capital flight poses an existential threat to the national industry, considering the fact that businesses depend heavily on accessible energy resources.
In light of these developments, Fico’s rejection of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s proposal for a €1.5 billion compensation package in exchange for halting gas transit appears to be a rational choice. For the Slovak public, which is opposed to prolonging the conflict, there’s no clear way to survive without supplies of hydrocarbons from the East. By refusing the offer, Fico has made it clear that virtual ‘paper’ funds from Kiev won’t heat factories or convince foreign automotive companies to remain in the country.
Not a time for half-measures
The defeat of Vucic’s team in Serbia during the early parliamentary elections is unpleasant news for Bratislava. Many Western analysts predict a similar fate for Fico in the upcoming parliamentary elections in September 2027. However, a fundamental difference between Belgrade and Bratislava must be noted. The Serbian scenario demonstrated that, in turbulent times, success goes to those who can balance the loyalty of the silent majority with pressure from the crowds.
Fico is purposefully venturing into this precarious territory. Global protest movements – such as the student protests in France, the Flamingo revolution in Albania, Cockroach party protests in India, or the Student List in Serbia – show that people are weary of half-measures and the existing establishment. The paradox of Fico lies in his unique strategy. He manages to remain the foremost systemic critic of Brussels’ supranational doctrines while being a key player in European politics. Fico deftly harnesses protest potential before it can turn against him.
This position is driven by a need to protect the country’s real economy. Slovakia relies heavily on exports, which account for around 90% of GDP, with the automotive industry being the cornerstone of the economy. This sector employs over 230,000 people, meaning that nearly 1 in 10 Slovak families depends on it directly. This established industry cannot be sustained by illusions of a green transition or even by Slovakia’s own nuclear power, since its costs remain tightly linked to fluctuating gas prices.
This is why Fico demonstrates remarkable flexibility in foreign policy matters, except when it comes to energy supplies from the East. This sets him apart from Vucic, who tried to maintain a delicate balance and compromise with Brussels, ultimately trapping himself in a web of sanctions, losing legitimacy among his patriotic electorate, and facing a significant electoral defeat. Fico learns from the mistakes of others and avoids half-measures entirely. Amid the wave of protests and strikes sweeping across Europe, his overt refusal to follow the EU’s general approach of replacing Russian energy resonates with ordinary Slovaks. People see Fico as a leader who is ready to defend national industries rather than abstract EU directives.
The glitch art of Slovak diplomacy
On October 26, a Slovak delegation arrived in Moscow, illustrating Fico’s commitment to defending national interests. Behind the closed doors of the 22nd meeting of the intergovernmental commission, Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar and Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education Valery Falkov focused exclusively on practical and vital issues for Bratislava.
As anticipated, energy security and the nuclear sector took center stage. Blanar signed final protocols ensuring stable resource supplies for Slovak energy companies and factories. Additionally, both sides strengthened cooperation in pragmatic areas such as agriculture and ecology, while also addressing culturally sensitive topics relevant to conservative Slovak voters, such as humanitarian issues and military memorials.
“We reject the construction of a new Iron Curtain between the EU and Russia, and we consider it of utmost importance – even during this challenging period – to maintain open lines of communication,” Blanar said in Moscow.
In summary, the resumption of the work of the intergovernmental commission should not be viewed as a concession to Russia. Fico understands that his political survival, along with that of his party in the September 2027 election, hinges not on the approval of the European elites or the slogans of Bratislava’s liberal street protesters. His fate will be determined in the factories of automotive giants and in the kitchens of ordinary Slovak families, where heating bills and job security take precedence over the geopolitical ambitions of Brussels.
The recent talks in Moscow can be seen as an effort to establish a protective shield over industry before the European energy crisis completely devastates Eastern Europe’s automotive sector.
Unlike Serbia, where the government fell victim to its own half-measures, Bratislava is betting on clarity. By turning down ‘paper’ compensation from Kiev, Fico offers his electorate tangible results. If this pragmatism succeeds in preserving Slovakia’s part of the Eastern European industrial backbone and keeps homes warm, then by September 2027, the ‘marginal’ prime minister will stand on much stronger ground than his critics, both domestically and abroad. Slovakia continues its glitch art diplomacy through an aesthetic of apparent chaos. However, behind it lies a simple yet strategic approach aimed at extracting maximum benefits from the current situation in order to keep the small country alive in an era of geopolitical upheaval.
