articles.title: Anduril unveils family of air defence interceptors
articles.body:
Anduril has revealed Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles built on a common two-stage architecture so that one production line can turn out versions for everything from point defence to upper-tier ballistic missile defence, according to the company.
The company set out the problem it is addressing, saying adversaries have invested in large volumes of low-cost, mass-producible offensive weapons and that air defence batteries are too often forced to expend exquisite interceptors against lower-cost threats, straining stores of the most critical defensive weapons and putting defenders on the losing side of the cost exchange.
Steelfin pairs a first-stage booster, which can take different solid rocket motors to suit range, launch configuration or packing density, with a second-stage terminal interceptor sharing the same airframe, avionics, software, flight control system and interfaces across every variant. Open interfaces between the subsystems in that terminal stage let different seekers and mission systems be fitted without redesigning the missile.
Because the variants share an architecture and components, they move through the same production line using the same tooling, technicians and facilities, and Anduril said it is planning to produce on the order of several thousand Steelfin variants a year in the short term, with capacity designed to flex to demand. The same open interfaces allow commercial off-the-shelf components and competition between vendors, widening the supplier base.
The missiles are compatible with launch infrastructure already in service, including the M903A2 launcher used by Patriot, the Mk 41 vertical launching system fitted to warships, Typhon and emerging containerised launchers, and are designed to integrate with fielded fire control systems such as Aegis and IBCS. Anduril has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles and will begin flight testing next year.
The American company has built a European presence over the past two years, with Latvia selecting its Barracuda cruise missile family and a United Kingdom arm working on autonomy, counter-drone systems and command software. Its approach of designing weapons around mass production and common components is the same argument being made by Helsing, which launched its own pair of low-cost interceptors this week.

articles.title: Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
articles.body:
Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
When Donald Trump returned triumphantly to the White House in January 2025, his supporters believed they could finally finish what he had started during his first term and reverse the Democrats’ social engineering agenda, commonly known as “wokeism”, curb illegal immigration, accelerate technological development and, above all, “make America great again”.
Trump moved quickly on the first two priorities, as he revoked 78 of Joe Biden’s executive orders, tightened border controls and gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) greater resources and powers to conduct raids in so-called sanctuary cities, where local authorities limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
But Trump’s determination to achieve everything at once, from restructuring the federal government and securing favorable trade deals to pursuing ambitions involving Greenland and Venezuela, has kept American politics in a state of turmoil, while his confrontational approach has also unsettled allies and opponents abroad.
The decision to launch joint military operations with Israel against Iran has proved particularly divisive as it’s fractured Trump’s conservative coalition, with some supporters accusing him of betraying his promise to end America’s “endless wars” and others fear the political consequences for Republicans in the approaching midterm elections.
The Iranian campaign has also hurt American consumers, given over the past year, petrol prices have risen by 38% and diesel by 71%, while food prices have increased by 2.5%.
The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz isn’t solely responsible, but Democrats and sympathetic media outlets have made it central to their criticism, while they also point to an increase of approximately $3.8 trillion in the national debt since Trump’s return, allegations of corruption within his administration and questions about the competence of senior officials, particularly Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
Republicans, including those who opposed the war with Iran, are trying to redirect voters towards the administration’s achievements as despite the turbulence, the US economy has grown by 3.2% since the end of 2024 and Investment is booming in certain sectors, particularly technology, while illegal crossings at the southern border have reportedly fallen by 95%.
Vice-President JD Vance, increasingly discussed as Trump’s potential successor, has urged Americans to give Republicans another chance, or at least another two years, to complete what they have begun, but for now, that opportunity appears uncertain. Yet contrary to some expectations, losing control of Congress wouldn’t necessarily spell disaster for Trump.
Even with Republican majorities in both chambers, he has preferred to govern through executive orders, issuing more than 290 since January 2025 and this is hardly unprecedented. Bill Clinton issued 364 over his eight years in office, including during periods when Republicans controlled Congress.
For presidents, demonstrating immediate effectiveness and scoring political points often matters more than ensuring continuity.
Democratic threats to impeach Trump and members of his administration may sound formidable, but removing officials from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate, a much higher hurdle and even if Democrats capture both chambers, converting their numerical advantage into meaningful political influence will not be straightforward.
They could, however, obstruct legislation, block nominations to senior administration positions and the federal judiciary, and subject the White House to sustained congressional scrutiny.
Their minimum objective would be to turn Trump into a lame-duck president for his remaining two years, but this strategy carries risks of its own because in the 2028 presidential campaign, Republicans could argue that Democrats prevented them from completing their programme.
For Moscow, however, the consequences of the midterms could be considerably more serious.
A Democratic-controlled Congress would almost certainly seek to complicate relations with Russia and there remains a strong desire in Washington to obstruct Trump’s apparent ambition for a new “Yalta” involving Russia, China and the United States. Equally persistent is the determination among influential American political circles to inflict a “strategic defeat” on Moscow.
This may help explain the Trump administration’s intensified diplomatic activity over Ukraine, given whatever opportunities exist for reaching an agreement today could narrow considerably after the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
Yet Washington’s urgency may also reflect an attempt to secure lasting advantages for itself before the political landscape changes.
The argument that there’s little time left, and that Moscow must therefore accept an agreement now or face worse conditions later, shouldn’t be allowed to overshadow Russia’s own interests.
Russia has an objective interest in normalizing relations with the United States, but any settlement must rest on mutually beneficial terms, rather than unilateral concessions extracted under the pressure of Washington’s electoral calendar.
Ultimately, as Americans prepare to vote in the midterms, Moscow should be concerned less with Trump’s political fortunes than with protecting its own interests.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

articles.title: Ukrainian postal service forms private air defense force, shoots down Russian drones
articles.body:
Ukrainian postal service forms private air defense force, shoots down Russian drones
Ukrainian postal and courier company Nova Poshta has started its own private air defense force and shot down Russian attack drones targeting their facilities, Vyacheslav Klymov, co-owner of the Nova group of companies, revealed at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on Oct. 26.
"We are one of the few companies that has implemented this project. I don't want to disclose the numbers, but we have destroyed 'Shahed' drones," Klimov said.
Nova Poshta is the largest private postal and courier company in Ukraine, operating over 15,817 branches across the country, and employing over 34,000 people. Its post offices and distribution centers have frequently come under Russian attack.
Despite the ongoing war, business is going well for Nova Poshta. The company quadrupled its net profit compared with last year, according to financial reports published on April 27.
Klimov also emphasised the importance of companies having their own private firefighting capabilities, rather than just waiting for the response of state authorities.
Nova Poshta employees frequently put out significant fires on their premises before the arrival of state emergency service firefighters, Klimov said.
"Now big businesses are looking for fire engines in Europe in order to create their own services. This is our property… who can forbid me from putting out a fire on my own territory?" he said.
Since late summer, Russia has been attacking Ukraine with jet-powered drones, adding to the now-familiar threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles. Between larger assaults, successive waves of jet-powered drones now arrive day and night.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.

articles.title: Russia replaces Ukrainians with Russian settlers in occupied Kherson Oblast; only 10–20% of pre-war population remains, Ukraine says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military intelligence estimates that only 10–20% of the prewar population may remain in the Russian-occupied left bank of Kherson Oblast, accusing Moscow of forcing Ukrainians from their homes while relocating Russian citizens to the area.
Russia’s efforts to displace Ukrainians and bring Russian citizens into occupied Kherson Oblast are part of Moscow’s broader campaign to consolidate control over occupied territory, impose Russian institutions, and erode Ukrainian national identity. Similar practices have been documented in other occupied Ukrainian territories, including the resettlement of Russians into homes in Mariupol and efforts to replace Ukrainian education with Russian curricula.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry (HUR) said Russia was creating intolerable living conditions for Ukrainian residents and unlawfully seizing private property to displace them. The agency said Moscow was simultaneously using financial incentives to recruit Russian teachers, doctors, and other professionals to work in occupied areas.
Russia brings in Russian workers as Ukrainians are pushed out
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, around 500,000 people lived on the left bank of Kherson Oblast, according to HUR. The agency estimates that only 10–20% of that population may remain.
Moscow is using state-backed recruitment programs, including “Zemsky Teacher,” “Zemsky Doctor,” “Zemsky Feldsher,” “Zemsky Cultural Worker,” and “Zemsky Coach,” to attract Russian citizens to occupied Ukrainian territory, HUR said.
Under these programs, Russian teachers and doctors who agree to work in occupied areas are offered one-time payments of 2 million rubles, while junior medical staff can receive 1 million rubles. The incentives also include higher salaries and other benefits, with contracts lasting at least five years.
HUR said hundreds of Russian teachers and doctors had already been brought to occupied Ukrainian territories from regions across Russia, including Krasnodar, Khabarovsk, Stavropol, and Perm Krais, as well as Rostov, Kursk, and Leningrad oblasts.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Russian medical personnel are needed primarily to serve occupying forces, while Russian teachers are being brought in to undermine Ukrainian children’s national identity.
Ukraine accuses Russia of war crimes and genocidal practices
HUR said Russia’s efforts to displace Ukrainian residents and bring in Russian citizens bore signs of war crimes and genocidal practices against the Ukrainian population.
The agency’s allegations concern both the coercive removal of Ukrainians from occupied territory and the replacement of local residents with people brought from Russia. Ukrainian authorities say these policies are part of Moscow’s broader effort to consolidate control over occupied Ukrainian land and impose Russian identity and institutions.
Kherson Oblast faces displacement, attacks, and a humanitarian crisis
Russian forces occupied much of Kherson Oblast in the early months of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian forces liberated the oblast’s right-bank areas, including the regional capital, in November that year, but Russia continues to occupy the left bank of the Dnipro River.
Russian forces regularly attack Ukrainian-controlled areas of Kherson Oblast with artillery and drones, killing and injuring civilians. Ukrainians have described repeated drone attacks on civilians as a “human safari.” In May 2025, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Russian forces’ repeated drone attacks on civilians along the Dnipro’s right bank amounted to crimes against humanity of murder.
The occupied town of Oleshky, on the left bank, has also faced severe shortages of food, medicine, and medical care amid restrictions on movement and continued fighting.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
Russia’s occupation has also exposed residents of Kherson Oblast to major humanitarian disasters. The destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023 flooded settlements along the Dnipro, including Russian-occupied communities on the left bank, damaging homes and forcing residents to flee. Russian forces’ restrictions on access and evacuation further endangered civilians in the affected areas.
While Russia occupies the left bank of Kherson Oblast, its forces continue to target civilians on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank. Across the oblast, residents face the consequences of Russia’s invasion, from forced displacement and property seizures under occupation to deadly drone and artillery attacks.
Read also
- Russia facilitates the resettlement of Russians to “abandoned” apartments in Mariupol
- Finland and Norway leaders make rare direct call to Putin, breaking with the West’s diplomatic isolation of the Russian leader to influence Ukraine peace talks
- Oleshky ceasefire expands beyond occupied town as truce holds without reported violations

articles.title: What Lula’s victory means for Palestine solidarity in Brazil
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What Lula’s victory means for Palestine solidarity in Brazil
Over the weekend, Brazilians elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva president once more by a very narrow margin, defying polls that had him trailing. No candidate had won a Brazilian runoff from second place since 1989. That precedent is broken, and it was broken from below: by student-led rallies in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Porto Alegre.
The rallies were called without Lula, by pop-star fan communities and influencers who injected energy into a campaign that had flagged all year, and by widespread mass communications like Deputy André Janones's WhatsApp channel, which passed 10 million followers. Many of those young figures have been vocal on Palestine. Their job now is to make sure their government hears them.
That mobilisation will matter all the more given the political landscape Lula faces. The Congress that convenes on 1 February will comprise 594 members, 513 deputies and 81 senators, with the right and its allies holding a comfortable majority in both houses. With 90 members close to the Palestinian struggle, the challenge will be to turn that support, alongside pressure from civil society, into concrete political action.
Palestine
Lula's words have been strong in recent years. He recognised the State of Palestine in 2010, the first in South America to do so, condemned the genocide in Gaza as early as October 2023, and did not back down when the Israeli colonial regime declared him persona non grata over his Holocaust comparison.
Brazil joined South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice and has had no ambassador in Tel Aviv since May 2024. His actions, however, were fewer. Diplomatic and trade relations with Israel were never fully cut. The Army’s planned purchase of 36 armoured howitzers from Elbit Systems was stalled in 2024 amid political opposition over military ties with Israel. The deal resurfaced in October 2026 after Brazilian defence company Avibras, reached an agreement with Elbit’s Brazilian subsidiary, AEL Sistemas, paving the way for local assembly.
The proposed purchase, worth almost $200 million, remained controversial after renewed public backlash, and the army subsequently cancelled the planned signing of the initial contract for two units. However, the wider procurement was not cancelled.
Lula has always been a conciliator. But a fourth and last term with popular backing opens room for much bolder steps, including ending trade relations with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, withdrawing from the Mercosur–Israel Free Trade Agreement, imposing a total embargo on weapons and technology transfers with the Zionist regime, and investigating and halting any indirect exports of Brazilian oil through third-country intermediaries.
The recognition of Palestine itself came at the end of his second term, and was then seen as his last.
For Palestinian solidarity movements, Lula’s victory above all means keeping the conditions they work under today, which are far more favourable than those a Flávio government would offer. The government remains open to dialogue with civil society, its own rhetoric lends legitimacy to the cause, and the state does not throw its weight behind the campaign against it.
Holding the line
Lula's government is not immune to Zionist lobbies, however. They continue to influence leaders close to the president and elected officials within his Workers' Party (PT) and Congress, where it needs centrist allies.
Even under Lula, part of the work will be to contest the government itself.
The institutional climate will remain turbulent. The reaction from Bolsonaro's supporters, especially if backed by Trump, is a challenge the PT anticipates. But the balance has shifted. Flávio will lose the privileged forum his Senate seat gives him, and with investigations advancing, he could face arrest.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, second in the family's line of command, is a fugitive in the United States after a Supreme Court justice issued an arrest warrant and cancelled his passports. He was sentenced to four years and two months for coercing the judicial process through lobbying Washington for sanctions against Brazilian magistrates.
From Florida, he has advised his brother to flee if defeated and joked about US Marines intervening. The family cannot hold political capital while their assets disperse.
Lula's path is to strengthen republican institutions – the Supreme Court included –, but he would be boxed in by a Senate taken over by the Bolsonarista party, which confirms justices and can impeach them.
Sustained public mobilisation in the streets and online could also help expose the networks of corruption and patronage that sustain the far-right’s power in Congress. Investigations into Banco Master and parliamentary budget amendments could weaken some of these networks and make it harder for politicians to convert economic power into political influence.
For the Palestinian movement, this matters. Challenging the interests that protect Zionist politicians is part of building a Congress more accountable to the public and less willing to enable complicity in the occupation.
Brazil’s importance in the region and to the cause is based on many factors; Brazil holds a third of Latin America's population and GDP, its main instrument abroad has never been economic or military might but diplomacy, and the country has built its influence on multilateralism, mediation and coalitions such as the BRICS. Gains made in Brazil tend to spread, as the wave of recognition of Palestine that followed 2010 showed.
In the region, Brazil is now an exception. Seven South American governments are aligned with Donald Trump, and Brazil is the largest country still holding out. Israel and the United States – as governments but also through Big Tech companies like META - invested here for years to change that. They have failed, for now.
Ultimately, a generation of young political figures carried this campaign, vocal on Palestine and with a strong presence online. In a contest increasingly fought on social media, a terrain the right had long dominated, the left has begun to close the gap. The platforms themselves are part of that dispute, and Meta's seeming interference in the campaign has become a matter of national and international debate.
The dispute over Brazil's public digital payment system (PIX) has also exposed US interest in challenging a model that threatens the dominance of American payment companies.
Furthermore, Brazil has a vibrant independent press that is often more receptive to the Palestinian cause. The country’s media landscape also includes major broadcasters such as TV Globo (formerly Rede Globo), Brazil’s largest television network and one of the country’s most influential media organisations. Its televised political debates attract large audiences and shape public discussion, with their coverage and political implications often resonating beyond Brazil’s borders.
Internationally, Lula's surprising victory and popular mobilisation must inspire and trickle to other countries where people are protesting in their masses against growing authoritarianism, fascism and neoliberal economic policies - all aligned with the Zionist regime - in France, India, Spain, and Serbia.
The pendulum is likely to swing in Brazil by 2030, and the next four years must be used to build irreversible actions toward liberation.
Rula Shadeed is the Co-Director of the Palestine Institute for Public Diplomacy.
Follow Rula on Instagram: @pipdbrasil and X: @rabetbypipd

articles.title: Ceasefire takes effect in Russian-occupied Oleshky ahead of planned civilian evacuation
articles.body:
A ceasefire has taken effect around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, located in Ukraine’s Kherson Region, as part of an agreed humanitarian operation to evacuate local residents. The ceasefire was announced by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and the Russian Defense Ministry.
Ukraine’s ombudsman wrote on Telegram:
“Today, at 3 a.m. Kyiv time and 4 a.m. Moscow time, a ceasefire was introduced in designated areas connected with the humanitarian mission.
This is taking place as part of a humanitarian mission that we are carrying out jointly with Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova, with the mediation and coordination of U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
The parties are observing the agreements that Yana Lantratova and I reached.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry also confirmed the ceasefire:
“In connection with preparations for a humanitarian operation in the area of the settlement of Oleshky in the Kherson region, the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation have ceased fire on the Kherson front and introduced a ‘regime of silence’ starting from 4 a.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27, 2026.”
As Lubinets previously said, before the evacuation begins, demining teams will first clear roads of explosives. Humanitarian aid will then be delivered to the city, and registration will begin for residents who want to leave Oleshky. The evacuation is expected to start only after those steps are completed.
The agreement on a ceasefire in Oleshky became public on Oct. 23. The White House announced it first, after which officials in Moscow and Kyiv confirmed the arrangement.
According to the latest estimates from Ukrainian authorities, about 2,000 people remained trapped in Oleshky under a complete blockade — without food, medical care, or a stable electricity supply. In addition to Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV had also joined the efforts to secure a humanitarian corridor for residents of the occupied city, calling Vladimir Putin from a hospital and asking him to halt the fighting in Oleshky as soon as possible.
In late September, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty called for an immediate ceasefire in occupied Oleshky in order to allow unhindered access for humanitarian organizations and the safe evacuation of civilians. He said the humanitarian crisis in the city was rapidly worsening and that civilians, including children, were trapped without adequate food, medical care, running water, or electricity.
In early October, Ukrainian officials reported that the country’s National Guard had carried out a successful operation to deliver humanitarian supplies to Russian-occupied Oleshky. Drones delivered about 400 packages weighing nearly 4 metric tons in total. The shipments contained food, medicine, and supplies for children.

articles.title: Kuwait sentences 3 to death over plot to kill first deputy PM
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Kuwait sentences 3 to death over assassination plot, 'working for Iran, Hezbollah'
A court in Kuwait has sentenced three men to death over an alleged plot to assassinate the country’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad al-Yusuf al-Sabbah, in a case involving charges of spying for Iran, joining Hezbollah and planning hostile acts against the state.
The Criminal Court’s State Security and Terrorism Division issued the sentences on Monday, while eight other defendants received prison terms.
Kuwaiti media reported that the eight were sentenced to five years in prison each. The verdicts are not final and can be appealed, according to Kuwait Times newspaper.
The three men sentenced to death were identified as Shia cleric Hussein Abdullah al-Maatouq, secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Hassan Abdulhadi Hajieh and Iranian national Abdulreza Haidar Dehqani, according to local media reports.
The defendants were convicted of charges including alleged harming of Kuwait’s national interests, collaborating with Iran, plotting to assassinate senior officials and joining the Lebanese Shia militant group Hezbollah, which Kuwait classifies as a terrorist organisation.
According to two judicial sources cited by AFP, one of the men sentenced to death had previously been convicted of terrorism in 2016 and later received an amnesty from the emir before being arrested again in April.
The prosecution said the case involved 11 defendants, including nine Kuwaitis, an Iranian national and another non-Kuwaiti. Three of the defendants were outside the country. It also said that three defendants had previously received final criminal sentences in state security cases in 2015 and 2017.
According to Kuwait’s Al-Qabas newspaper, prosecutors accused the defendants of attempting to use explosives to carry out the assassination plot. One defendant was separately accused of attempting to bring explosives into the country to enable the others to carry out the alleged operation.
In its reasoning, the court said the defendants had sought to undermine Kuwait’s security, spread social unrest and erode public confidence in the authorities’ ability to protect lives and property.
Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai reported that the indictment accused the defendants of seeking assistance from and communicating with Iran and groups acting in its interests, including Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on 28 February, at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
The indictment also accused the defendants of joining and participating in a banned organisation, knowingly supporting its objectives and spreading ideas intended to undermine the country’s fundamental political and social systems through unlawful means.
Prosecutors further alleged that the defendants had engaged in activities harmful to Kuwait’s national interests, including attempting to use explosives to carry out the assassination and cause public panic. One defendant was accused of attempting to procure explosives to enable the others to commit the alleged crimes.
The court’s ruling is subject to appeal.
In March, Kuwait announced the arrest of dozens of people it said were linked to Hezbollah and plotting attacks in the Gulf state, which was repeatedly targeted by Iranian missiles and drones after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a regional war.
Hezbollah, engaged in conflict with Israel for more than three years, has denied it has a presence in Kuwait.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian ammunition and supply depots in occupied territories – General Staff
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck Russian ammunition and logistics depots, concentrations of weapons and military equipment, and personnel in Russian-occupied parts of Luhansk, Donetsk and Zaporizhia regions on Monday and overnight into Tuesday, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said on Facebook on Tuesday.
Ammunition depots near Diakove in Luhansk region and Ohorodnie in Donetsk region were hit, along with a concentration of Russian weapons and military equipment near Krasnohorivka in Donetsk region.
Russian logistics depots were also struck near Luhansk, Antratsyt and Tymonove in Luhansk region.
Ukrainian forces additionally attacked concentrations of Russian personnel near Lahidne and Antratsyt in Luhansk region and near Novopetrivka in Zaporizhia region.
The General Staff said the strikes on ammunition stocks would reduce Russian forces' firepower at the front, while the destruction of logistics supplies would complicate resupply for Russian units.
It said operations against key Russian military targets would continue until Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine ended.
